en: [The Śrī Bṛhaspati Smṛti] In former times, men were devoted to dharma and non-violent; legal procedure was introduced for those overcome by greed and hatred. (Br̥h 1.1.1)
If the master offers wages to the servants who perform their work, but the servants do not perform it, then a dispute arises therein. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.2)
Someone may commit violence, or one may fail to give what is due;
these two are the grounds for dispute, and between them, the latter has more frequent occurrences.
When a substance is sold and taken for the purpose of repaying a debt, that price paid by the creditor is known as *vyavahāra* (legal transaction). (Br̥haspati 1.1.4)
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.1: Royal Qualities] Therefore, I shall describe the duties and qualities of a king in their proper order:
the creditor, the debtor, the one in doubt, the surety, the document, and the witnesses. Br̥h 1.1.5.
Listen to the origin of him who reflects correctly upon Soma,
Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vitta, Āpatti, and Yama.
Having extracted the mere essence of fire, the form of the King was indeed fashioned;
from him all beings, both moving and stationary, were produced.

Out of fear, people are able to pursue their livelihoods and do not deviate from their own duties; for in a kingless state, there can be no agriculture, commerce, lending at interest, or protection of property.
Therefore, he was created in ancient times as the leader of the social classes and stages of life. Legal procedure consists of two categories: that arising from property and that arising from injury.
The basis of wealth consists of fourteen [factors], while that based on violence is fourfold:
two types of harshness, killing, and likewise the abduction of another's wife.

Laziness, withholding what has been deposited, failing to rise when others assemble, failure to provide for dependents, lack of service, false claims regarding land, and selling what one does not own; Brh_1.1.11.
Remorse regarding purchase and sale, breach of contract, the union of man and woman, theft, partition of inheritance, and gambling with dice. Bṛhaspati 1.12.
These fourteen words, which originate from their meanings,
are further divided in this way into many tens according to the distinctions in their functions.
Harsh speech, violence, and likewise the abduction of another's wife— Bṛhaspati has thus declared these four to be the very grounds for the arising of injury.
Distinguished individually as inferior, middling, and superior,
the specific distinction of these four is likewise set forth in their proper order.
These eighteen points set forth in the treatises on Dharma are indeed the root of all disputes; those who know them are the true investigators.
The first quarter is known as the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), and likewise the second is the reply (uttara).
The third quarter is to be stated as the application (kriyāpāda), and the fourth is the final decision (nirṇaya).
In a matter of doubt, a decision is declared to be of four kinds: by means of dharma, by legal procedure, by conduct, and by the king’s command. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.18)
That legal proceeding in which a decision is made by relying solely upon the treatises (śāstra) should be understood as a judicial transaction (vyavahāra); through it, too, Dharma increases.
A definitive conclusion is reached there by means of inference based on local custom and what is accepted by the people; however, in such a case, the formal legal procedure is overridden.
When a king, setting aside established custom, issues a new decree, that royal command prevails; by it, the established custom is superseded. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.21)

In accordance with the Dharmaśāstras, the king— free from anger and greed, truthful, and having his senses under control— should, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, examine legal cases for the sake of protecting his subjects. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.1.22)
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.4: The Section on Dharma] That which consists of seven constituent elements belonging both to the seeker of victory and to the enemy—
this is what they call the fourteenfold circle of states.
The four guardians of the earth, together with their eight individual friends, as well as the ministers and others—these are composed of syllables in this world. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.24)
Having risen in the morning and performed purification according to the rules,
the king [should honor] his gurus, astrologers, physicians, gods, brahmins, and domestic priests.
Having honored these [guests] as is appropriate with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments,
and having greeted his teachers and elders, he should enter the assembly hall with a cheerful countenance.
The king, having entered the most excellent assembly hall, should examine the affairs of state while seated or standing, surrounded by exactly three virtuous men.
For the protection of his accumulated self, wife, wealth, and subjects,
the king should cause a fortress to be built, provided with two encircling walls.
It was filled with kings who provided fuel, liquids, cane, grass, food, and mounts,
as well as various machines and weapons, and was accompanied by affectionate, heroic men.
Having summoned Brahmins learned in the Vedas and Kṣatriyas who maintain the sacred fire-offerings,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
Irrevocable taxes should be granted to them, as well as house-sites;
having recorded this in their own edicts, they should be made exempt from royal dues.

They should perform the daily rites, the occasional rites, those for specific desires, as well as those for pacification and prosperity; likewise, they should carry out the ancient rituals and the disciplinary measures for those whose conduct is doubtful.
Wherever the ground is level or even uneven,
the hall, the ramparts, the moats, and so forth should be constructed accordingly.
Then the subjects should construct houses all around there; likewise, the twice-born, Vaiśyas, Vaiśyas, artisans, craftsmen, and guards [should do so].
One should likewise arrange for the placement of gates, exits, roundabouts, pits, crossroads, assembly grounds, marketplaces, and cattle pens.
How can one who was proclaimed "virtuous" and celebrated in the assembly of people be described as "devoid of virtue" by that very same mouth?
Therefore, one should not disturb the authority or the livelihood of one who is faultless;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of infinite regress, and likewise, the support [of the community] would perish.
Having properly settled his territory and constructed fortifications according to the treatises,
he should constantly apply his supreme strength toward the removal of thorns.
That protection of the subjects is declared by those who know the law to be threefold:
[protection] from the enemy's army, from the fear of thieves, and from the powerful who act unjustly.
The king should pacify the fear caused by the enemy's army through strategic means,
and he should daily provide justice for those who have been oppressed by the powerful.
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one offers oblations, and whatever one worships—
the king becomes entitled to a sixth part of that by virtue of providing protection.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices day after day with hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees.
A cultivator shall give a tenth, an eighth, or a sixth part of the produce from fallow land, from land sown in the rainy season, and from land sown in the spring, respectively, to the king.
They should offer oblations to the spirits according to local custom every six months or annually;
this is declared to be the ancient law for farmers.
[The manner of constructing the assembly hall:

Within the fortress, one should build separate houses—whether near water, on a mountain, in a grove, in a marshy area, or in a desert—that are surrounded by water and trees. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.7 [and 1.1.45].
To the east of that [place], he should construct an auspicious assembly hall facing the east,
provided with garlands, incense, and seats, and furnished with seeds and gems.
It should be provided with images, paintings, and deities, as well as fire and water;
it should be auspiciously marked, characterized by the features prescribed in the treatises on architecture (vāstuśāstra).
Having occupied the auspicious seat, with his limbs properly covered and his mind concentrated,
he should pay homage to the world-protectors and begin the examination of the case.
The Brahmin is the root of the tree of Dharma; the king is its trunk and branches;
the ministers are its leaves and flowers; and protection through justice is its fruit.
Fame, wealth, the essence of fruits, enjoyment, acquisition, and honor;
invincibility, standing in the ranks of the world, and an eternal station in heaven.
Having become impartial toward these juices of justice,
and having abandoned greed and other such passions, the king should carry out the determination of the law through adjudication.
The king himself should preside over disputes concerning livelihoods;
he is served by the learned according to the path seen in the scriptures.
Therefore, a king should protect [his subjects] properly and with diligent effort according to justice;
thereby he shall obtain wealth, sovereignty, and vast fame.
In brief, the gods know truth and human beings know falsehood;
he whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.
The sacrifice arises from the conjunction of the animal, the clarified butter, the officiating priests, and so forth;
just as it is connected with these, so too is its conventional usage explained.
However, one who reaches a decision on legal matters by relying upon the opinions of the judge and the court members through the application of proper reasoning incurs no punishment.
The assembly is declared to be of four kinds: the established, the unestablished, the sealed, and likewise the disciplined; and the members of the assembly are of the same types.
Established in the city and in the village, she is named "The Moving One" yet is "Unestablished";
she is sealed, conjoined with direct perception, associated with kingship, and is the ruler.
One who has perfected his intellect should observe the principles of logic; that assembly is equal to a sacrificial rite.
The members of the assembly (sabhyas) should be knowers of the worlds, the Vedas, their auxiliary sciences, and the Dharma—whether they be seven, five, or even three.
That assembly hall, where the foremost of Brahmins were seated, was like unto a sacrificial rite itself.
The king should always ensure that the plaintiff and the defendant are protected by guarantors;
this is the tenfold administration of justice upon which the monarch should preside.
Having set aside one-eighth part of the day, he should go to sleep;
that time is remembered as the supreme period for legal proceedings according to the vision of the scriptures.
The king should appoint as members of the assembly those who are engaged in performing virtuous deeds, devoted to truth and righteousness, free from anger and greed, and learned in the scriptures.
There should be seven, five, or three members of the assembly.
Those who are ignorant of local customs, atheists, those devoid of scriptural knowledge,
and those who are insane, angry, greedy, or afflicted by pain— these should not be questioned in reaching a definitive decision.
The king, or else a learned Brahmin acting as the presiding judge, shall examine the cases,
having placed at the forefront the constituent elements of justice and remaining steadfast in the opinion of the court members and the sacred scriptures.
Because he delights the subjects by means of the fourfold army and shines with his own physical splendor, he is therefore designated as a "rāja" (king).
Legal procedure has been declared by the wise to be manifold, though it is essentially one;
the king and the learned Brahmin are the ones who bring about its final determination.
The Śruti declares that he who asks the question regarding a matter based on legal procedure is called *prāṭ*;
he who adjudicates therein is known as the *prāḍvivāka*. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.68)
In a legal dispute, he asks the question and likewise the counter-question;
because he speaks first with kindness, he is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka*.
Accompanied by the chief justice, his ministers, the Brahmins and the royal chaplain, and the members of the assembly, the king remains in heaven through his righteous conduct as a witness to dharma.

He should appoint as a minister a twice-born Brahmin who understands the meaning of all treatises, is free from greed, speaks with justice, is wise, and has been reached through hereditary succession.
He who, setting aside the twice-born, should look after affairs together with the low-born (vṛṣalas),
his kingdom flows away and his army and treasury perish.
For those who wander in the forest, their ritual practice should take place in the forest;
likewise, for soldiers it is in the army, and for merchants it is on the trade caravans.
For plowmen, artisans, wrestlers, usurers, guilds,
ascetics, and thieves, the decision shall be made according to their own specific laws.
Families, guilds, assemblies, and the appointed king are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding. (Bṛhaspati 1.1.75)
However, he should have the affairs of ascetics carried out by those learned in the three Vedas,
and likewise by those who know the application of illusion (māyā-yoga), and not by himself, for fear of provoking anger.
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
Whether it be a brother, a son worthy of honor, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle, there is no one who,
having deviated from his own duty, is not subject to punishment by the king.
Where there may be no learned Brahmin, one should employ a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; but one should avoid a Śūdra with great effort.
But one who is devoid of righteous conduct and actions, and lacks the characteristics of a Brahmin,
yet says "I am a Brahmin"— him they call a "Brahmin-claimant" (brāhmaṇabruva).
The king should appoint as astrologer and scribe those who know the true nature of words and their designations, who are skilled in calculation, pure, and proficient in various scripts.
In cases where there is no motive for malice, and in matters concerning protection, witnesses, or litigants,
that man who speaks the truth must be appointed as a judge, subject to the authority of the court members.
That assembly hall, presided over by a king who, having established his mind, examines legal cases according to this tenfold procedure, is equal to a sacrificial rite.

Among these, the king is remembered as the head; the presiding judge is the mouth; the members of the court are the arms; the legal code is the hands; and the astrologer and the scribe are the shanks.
The eyes are like gold, fire, and water; the heart and the feet are likewise the self-manifest person (svapuruṣa).
Indeed, the king should place gold, fire, water, and the treatises on dharma— those things which are meritorious and beneficial— in the midst of them.
One should visualize the Sun, the Moon, the gods, and so forth, as well as the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) there;
indeed, gold, fire, water, and one's own person are the ten limbs of the practice.
And the specific function of each of these ten has been declared separately:
the king is the presiding speaker and the instructor; the courtier is the examiner of the case.
Smṛti declares the decision regarding victory, the awarding of the prize, and likewise punishment;
for the purpose of an oath, gold, fire, and water are used when there are thirsty creatures present.
The accountant shall calculate the matter, and the scribe shall record the legal procedure;
his own attendants shall summon the parties, the petitioners, the members of the court, and the witnesses.
The punishment of speech and the punishment of reproach depend upon the Brahmins,
while both the punishment of fines and the punishment of death are said to depend upon the king.
Those families, guilds, assemblies, and so forth, who are properly known by the king,
shall carry out the legal affairs of men, excluding acts of violence and injustice.
The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies are declared to be the makers of final decisions;
a matter that has not been deliberated upon by the families must be decided by the guilds.
That which is unknown to the guilds and the corporations is known by the officials;
the members of the court are superior to the families and other such groups, and the presiding officer is declared to be superior even to them.
The king is superior to all because he diligently determines the Dharma through the adjudication of disputes among the highest, the lowest, and those of middle rank.
The cognitions of the Lord, moving ever higher above all other cognitions,
[perceive those] possessed by the darkness of ignorance and covered by the film of doubt.
He who makes the scriptures free from defects by means of the probe of the collyrium of learning attains fame in this world, honor from kings, and a destination in heaven.

He who, having abandoned greed, hatred, and the like, should carry out the determination of legal matters according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
But the members of the court must not overlook an action that has proceeded unrighteously;
by overlooking it, those kings go headlong to hell.
But having recognized that the king's mind has strayed from the path of justice, one must speak what is unpleasant there; for a member of the assembly who does not do so is a sinner.
A member of the assembly should speak words consistent with dharma and artha;
if the king does not listen, then that member of the assembly is indeed blameless.
If the judge should hold secret consultations with the plaintiff regarding matters that have not yet been decided,
he too shall be punished, and the members of the court all the more so.
Whether through negligence, ignorance, delusion, or even greed,
if a member of the assembly speaks falsely on any matter, he is considered by tradition to be an unfit member and should be punished.
Where there is no document, no witness, and no possession—
where no means of proof exist— the king alone is the authority in that case.
Those doctrines which cannot be determined and whose nature is doubtful—
the king shall be the authority regarding them, since he is the lord of all.
Every day, surrounded by his courtiers, he should personally oversee the legal proceedings.
Those members of the court who speak unjustly, as well as those who live on bribes and those who deceive the person of confidence— all of them must be banished.
Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the treatises is qualified to speak;
whatever he declares in the assembly is the Dharma—of this there is no doubt.
The king should sit facing the east, while the members of the court face the north;
the calculator faces the west, and the scribe faces the south.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come, so must subjects be restrained by the king; for that indeed is the vow of Yama.
Without contradicting the Dharmaśāstras and the Arthaśāstra, the king,
examining the course of legal proceedings with skill, should guide them.
But when the members of the assembly here deviate from the science of logic (nyāyaśāstra) and reach a decision, then dharma, being violated, destroys everyone; of this there is no doubt.
The treatises of Manu and others are to be upheld, but never the treatises on worldly affairs (artha-śāstra).
When there is a conflict between the two, one must act according to the words declared in the Dharma-śāstra.
A final decision should not be made by relying on the scriptures alone;
for if an inquiry is devoid of reasoning, the loss of dharma arises.
Having occupied that [throne] in the forenoon, he should look upon it with his aged ministers and dependents,
and likewise listen to the ancient treatises on dharma and artha.
A thief may become a non-thief, and a virtuous man an unvirtuous one, through legal proceedings;
without logical investigation, Māṇḍavya was treated as a thief.
The unreal appears like the real, and the real appears like the unreal;
they are seen as producers of delusion. Therefore, one should investigate by means of reasoning.
In sacrifice Viṣṇu is worshipped; in worldly affairs, the lord of the earth;
here, the victor is the sacrificer, while the defeated is declared to be the sacrificial animal.

The prima facie argument and the rejoinder are the opening [acts]; the proposition is remembered as the oblation; the three Vedas and the treatises are the members of the assembly; and self-restraint is the sacrificial fee for the officiating priests.
In the same way, the calculator and the scribe should be understood as the two witnesses;
this legal procedure, thus collected, is declared to be equal to a sacrificial rite.
When one, unassailable by others because he follows a path consistent with traditional conduct and mindfulness,
brings a matter before the king, that indeed constitutes a legal subject for litigation.
A plaint made by one who is an outcaste or similar person, one who has not returned to his natural state,
or one made by someone lacking independence, does not succeed.
A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by illness, distressed, a child, or an elderly person,
as well as one concluded with an unrelated party, is not valid.
Between teacher and pupil, father and son, husband and wife, or master and servant— among these who are united in such relationships, a legal dispute is not valid.
The members of the court should cause the plaintiff's case to be recorded only after it has been thus examined;
however, they shall not adjudicate a dispute that is unproven or one that is detested by the people.

Likewise, the customs of regions and castes must be maintained; those duties which have been established for those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), as well as for those dwelling in difficult terrains,
and for specific regions, castes, families, and so forth, should be observed.
In that very same way, those subjects must be protected; otherwise, they become agitated.
When people become alienated, both the army and the treasury perish.
In the South, twice-born men marry the daughters of their maternal uncles;
in the Middle Country, laborers and artisans eat beef.
In the east, men were eaters of fish and women were devoted to adultery;
in the north, women were drinkers of liquor and menstruating women were touchable by men. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.129)
Those born together [as twins] take as their wife the brother's widow who has no husband;
by this act, they are not worthy of being subjected to penance.
Because they constantly fail to perform what is enjoined and because they indulge in what is forbidden,
the king should provide them with food and clothing and take the remainder as his own.
Those born of inverse unions, as well as those dwelling in impure regions, must be protected with effort according to the treatises; however, in cases of doubt, she alone is the means of proof.
Having seen that [document], the court should reach a decision according to the previously established rule regarding the customary toll,
fines, and the monthly or six-monthly tax.
A boundary should always be established in writing and supervised by merchants;
the claims of both the plaintiff and the defendant must be heard.
Having examined the matter, one should take action; otherwise, one shall go to hell. (Br̥haspati Smr̥ti 1.134)
When one person engages in debate with many people, including women and spectators,
his argument is declared by those who know the Dharma to be inadmissible.
Those who are not to be obstructed [in their passage] include: one intent on a sacrificial session (sattra), one engaged in a wedding, a sick person, those afflicted by grief, the insane, children,
the intoxicated, the elderly, one who is being questioned, one occupied with royal business, and one observing a vow.
A soldier in battle, a farmer during the harvest, those in a state of distress, and likewise women accompanied by a protector, must not be obstructed when near [the king].
An envoy who has not yet attained legal capacity, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow,
those in a precarious situation, and likewise women accompanied by a protector, shall not be obstructed.
But when the grain has grown, the merchant who has sold his merchandise, the farmer,
and likewise those who were intent on their work, shall be made to pay once their transactions are completed.
When one's mind is unable to engage in a dispute even though one wishes to do so,
time should be granted to him by both the plaintiff and the defendant.
The king should cause that very person against whom one brings a charge— whether on the basis of truth or even out of suspicion— to be summoned by means of a female messenger or a male servant.
In the case of those who are timid, dull-witted, insane, elderly, women,
children, or diseased, a kinsman, an appointed official, or another person may state the preceding and subsequent statements.
When appointed as a priest in a debate, both [the priest and his opponent] are proclaimed to be equal;
through the sacrifice, the master obtains merit, while in the debate he obtains either loss or victory.
But if one who has been summoned does not come out of arrogance, even though supported by the strength of his kinsmen,
the judge shall determine a fine for him in accordance with the nature of the legal claim.

At the proper time, he should question the petitioner who stands before him with a bowed head: "What is your business? What is your distress? Do not fear; speak, O man! (Bṛhad-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.145)

When he has been questioned in this manner, the members of the court, together with the Brahmins, should deliberate upon what he says; if it is found to be just, then he should thereafter be summoned for the purpose of the trial.
He should provide a seal so that he may command either a document or a person.
If one who has been summoned, being capable, should disregard the king’s decree,
the judge shall determine his punishment in accordance with the nature of the legal charge.

In cases involving those who are immature, elderly, or infirm, or those distressed by irregular medical treatment, the fine for an inferior offense shall be fifty; for middling offenses, it shall be at least one hundred;
and for serious matters, he shall always be subject to a fine of at least five hundred.
In a region struck by an enemy army, or afflicted by famine or disease,
one should perform a reconquest but should not inflict punishment.
Those who are addicted to the neglect of their duties, and those agitated by the king's business and festivities.
A king should not summon servants who are intent on mischief, those who act deceitfully toward his prosperity, or those who are intoxicated, insane, or negligent.
Neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor one acting under a legal mandate,
shall be exempt from punishment when speaking falsely in judicial proceedings while testifying on behalf of another.
A young woman born of a noble family who has not yet had a child, even if she is the best among all castes, is considered to have been enjoyed by her paternal kinsmen. // Brh_1.1.153 //
Having understood the time and place, as well as the strength and weakness of the matters at hand,
the king should gradually cause even those who are incapable of calculation and the like to be summoned by means of vehicles.
The invitation of those whose husbands are dependent on them, of wanton women, of courtesans, of those who have lost their family status, and of those who are outcastes is prescribed.
A guarantor capable of determining the outcome of the case should be accepted from both parties.
Having learned of their intent, even those who have gone forth as forest-dwellers and the like,
the king should summon them for important affairs without causing them offense.
The plaintiff shall restrain one who does not abide by the matter to be stated or who departs from it,
until the appearance for summons.

Restriction may be of four kinds: restriction to a place, restriction by time, restriction from travel, and likewise restriction from occupation; one who is restricted must not violate that restriction. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.159)
Fields, gardens, houses, and so forth, as well as wealth, grain, and the like—
these must be restrained from litigants who speak unrighteously.
But if one who has been placed under restraint should himself voluntarily relinquish that restraint,
there is no fault arising from his transgression, nor shall a fine be imposed upon him.
After reporting [the matter] to the king, one who has been placed under restraint shall not release himself on his own accord;
if he should release himself, he must be made to pay a fine, and one under restraint shall not violate the restrictions.
In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, or encountering a calamity in a difficult region,
one who has not yet accomplished his purpose incurs no fault by overstepping a prohibition.

One who desires to marry, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to perform a sacrifice, one beset by calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one engaged in royal business—[these may eat on the sabbath]. Br̥had-Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.164b.

Cowherds [should attend] when the cattle are grazing; farmers, at the commencement of the crops; artisans, at their respective times; and those who bear arms, during battle. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.165)
Those who have climbed a tree or a mountain, those situated on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats,
and all those in difficult positions— these must not be obstructed by those intent on accomplishing their task.
But he who restrains one who is not subject to restraint by means of suppressing the senses, or by withholding food, breath, and so forth, shall be punished; however, he does not commit an offense.
One who is subject to restraint deserves punishment for evading it;
however, one who restrains someone who is not subject to restraint must be punished by the king—this is the established rule.

The king should examine the arguments of litigants who have come before him and are disputing repeatedly; he should not consider arguments fabricated by himself, nor those merely reported by his officials.

When one who has been oppressed comes of his own accord seeking redress through legal instruments, the judge, or a representative, should question him slowly and steadily. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.13; 1.1.170)
The statement of one who acts without being authorized because he has not been granted the right to transact shall not be accepted, except in the case of what is written or sent.
When the plaintiff and the defendant arrive one after the other,
the trial should be conducted according to the order of their castes, or else by considering whose grievance is more urgent.
Those afflicted by great sins, those driven by madness or intoxication,
as well as the mentally dull, the very elderly, and children, should be known as those who are exempt from [legal] censure.

A position that has been declared as unacceptable, as well as a disputant who is unanswerable—such a disputant and such a position must not be accepted; I shall now explain what kind of disputant and what kind of position should be accepted.
When a proponent, intent on establishing his own position, speaks what he intends to say by resorting to an extreme degree of distress, that is called the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument).
The plaint, the reply, the proof, and likewise the decision;
legal procedure consists of these four parts.
"False rejoinder," "counter-attack," and likewise "prior judgment"—these four types of replies have been declared by those learned in the treatises. (Br̥hadāranyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.2)
In cases of falsehood, in a counter-attack, and likewise in a plea of prior judgment, that [trial] is to be known as having four legs; in cases of admission, it has two legs.
But he who, though being urged by various means, does not give an answer,
is considered defeated after seven nights have passed and deserves punishment.

[Br̥h 1.2.1 Definition of the Thesis] Once that [opponent] has been present, the proponent should formulate a thesis that is faultless, accompanied by a proposition, and endowed with means of valid cognition and authoritative tradition. Br̥h 1.2.5.
One should record the country, location, year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste,
the quantity of goods, the number, the profit, the suffering, and the characteristics of the debtor.
Whatever point one may advance, one should not lead it into contradiction, nor should one shift to another position; by doing so, one falls away from the previous one.
A king should avoid a thesis that is unestablished, faulty, purposeless, useless, impossible to prove, or contradictory. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.2; 1.2.8)
That which has not been created by anyone is declared to be "unestablished" (aprasiddha).
It is proclaimed as faulty when it has a different meaning [than intended], lacks its own proper meaning, or is defective. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.9)
That which involves a minor offense and a minor purpose is known as "insignificant" (nirarthaka);
however, that which is devoid of any obstruction to the accomplishment of the task should be understood as "purposeless" (niṣprayojana).
A legal proceeding devoid of such grounds as indolence and the like is considered meaningless;
likewise, one that involves verbal abuse, physical assault, and so forth, should be understood as purposeless.
"He must give me a bow made of hare's horn"—
the wise say that such a position is impossible and unachievable.
That case in which, once it has been presented, opposition arises against the judge, the king, the city, or the kingdom, is declared to be "contradictory" (viruddha).

Those who know the subject matter of a thesis recognize the *pakṣa* (the position to be proved) as being free from defects of the proposition, endowed with valid reasons, well-ascertained, and established in the world.
It consists of very few syllables yet contains abundant meaning; it is free from ambiguity and confusion;
it is liberated from contradictory causes and serves as a refutation of opposing views.

For in formal debates, when disputants must speak without confusion, it is the statement that constitutes the proposition (pratijñā), while its meaning constitutes the subject of the thesis (pakṣatā). 1.2.16.
Whether out of delusion or through deceit, that which was not stated by the proponent,
even if it is included within the rejoinder, should be accepted by both parties.
Having correctly reflected upon such qualities as these and reached a firm conviction, one should adopt a position that is worthy of acceptance; otherwise, it is a fallacious position.
A thesis that is devoid of place and time, lacking in substance and number, and deficient in the measure of what is to be proven, is considered unacceptable.
If the initial plea is written down as being based on false reasoning, devoid of legal action, concerning an impossible matter, or confused,
the defeat in the lawsuit arises.
The plaintiff who, having stated a charge, passes over it and speaks of another,
or who, having stated a line of action, speaks otherwise, shall suffer defeat.
In the first stage, the plaintiff shall clear up any deficiency or excess,
until the defendant, in the presence of the assessors, has provided his answer.
In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife,
or other indecent accusations, no counter-accusation is permitted.
In the case of killing a human, theft, violating another's wife, eating what is forbidden to eat, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden; Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.24.
In cases of harsh speech, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, the informant shall not be made to pay; rather, the perpetrator himself shall plead the case.
The debate consisting of eighteen points has been presented for deliberation;
there are other points here as well, which the king himself may investigate.

Taking one-sixth [of the produce], receiving pure [gifts], not transgressing agreements, finding treasure-troves, killing, confiscation, theft, and violating a prohibition or a royal edict; Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.2.27.
The king, or his official, should not personally initiate a legal case;
rather, he should reduce excessive claims and fulfill those that are deficient.
One should record [the testimony] on the ground as long as the matter has not been fully determined—
whether it be what was heard, what was written, what was corrected, or what was deliberated upon.
Then the judge shall cause the plaintiff's case, as stated by himself, to be written on a wooden board with chalk;
thereafter, it shall be refined and written upon the official document.
But for those who, once the matter has been presented and accepted, settle their dispute among themselves,
one should determine a fine for them in accordance with the nature of the accusation.
Furthermore, those cases involving those who oppose cities, villages, or great kings,
as well as all matters that are not fit to be granted, are declared to be inadmissible lawsuits.
One should first write on a wooden board or on the ground using chalk; having corrected any omissions or excesses, one should subsequently inscribe it upon a leaf.
When the plaintiff, due to lack of confidence, does not venture to speak,
time should be granted to him in accordance with his capacity and the nature of the case.
If [the judge] is unable to settle the dispute between two parties who wish to litigate,
then a period of time must be granted to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is fourfold, and likewise the counter-argument (pratipakṣa);
the final determination (nirṇaya) is said to be fourfold, though some maintain it is eightfold.
The country, the time, as well as the place and the layout,
the designation of the knower, the dwelling, the measurement, and the name of the field.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should cause these ten items to be recorded: [the names of] the father and grandfather, and the proclamation of former kings.
Or he may obtain a postponement for three days or even seven days,
as long as it takes for the thought to arise in him who wishes to speak in the dispute.
Even a case involving many assertions that has been settled in legal proceedings,
the king may, if he desires to discover the truth, certainly take it up again.
Accusation based on suspicion, the truth, a request regarding the matter at hand,
and a renewed legal proceeding once a case has been concluded— these are to be known as the fourfold types of plaints.
Delusion is defined as doubt; it is the certain perception of a lost object.
Delusion is also the solicitation for an object already obtained, as well as the repeated performance of actions regarding what has already been done. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.42)
But he who has been expelled by the king, or he who causes opposition among the citizens, or likewise among the whole kingdom and its constituent subjects; ||| Brh_1.2.43 |||
He who does not wish to act justly, or who acts unjustly,
and likewise he who does not cause [the matter] to be recorded in writing— his case shall not succeed.
One should avoid from afar that position in which both contradictory and non-contradictory meanings are seen to be established within a single [subject]. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.45)
But when such a position has been formulated by the proponent, the opponent should then offer a rejoinder connected to that position. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.1)
Once the prima facie argument has been determined, distinguished by what is to be accepted and what is not to be accepted,
and established as a formal proposition, one should then cause the rejoinder to be written down.
Where one requests time due to timidity,
fear, opposition, or confusion of memory, there one deserves to obtain this [time]. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.3)

Depending on one's capacity, one may receive [the gift] for one day, three days, five days, seven days, or even a fortnight, a month, three months, four months, or a year. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.4)
Those who know this declare that an answer which pervades the position, which is essential, free from doubt, unconfused, and not requiring further explanation, is truly understood. Brh_1.3.5.
The reply (uttara) is of four kinds: the inadmissible (sāmpratam), the false (mithyā), the plea of prior judgment (prāṅnyāya), and the plea of a special cause (kāraṇa). Br̥haspati 1.3.6.
But he who does not give a reply according to the facts during the plaintiff's case must be compelled to pay by means of conciliation and other such methods, even if he is a witness.

Kindly speech preceded by affection, conciliation, sowing dissension, and the display of fear; the deprivation of wealth, as well as corporal punishment and imprisonment—these constitute the methods of force.
Bṛhaspati states that in cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusations regarding cattle, or a grave emergency, one may litigate over land immediately, even outside the prescribed season.

One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the performance of the act, one who does not present himself, one who is unable to provide an answer, and one who flees when summoned— these are recorded as the five kinds of defeated parties.
In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, acts of violence, fraud, and false testimony, one should institute a lawsuit immediately.
In the case of a cow, a bull, a field, women, and procreation;
likewise in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, as well as in buying and selling.
In a plea of prior judgment and in a plea of justification, the defendant shall point out the evidence;
but in a plea of denial, the plaintiff shall do so, while in a plea of admission, it is not possible [for either party to produce evidence].
When a proponent advances a position without stating a reason, that should be known as a "pratipatti" (an admission); however, a reason is a distinct matter, namely the "uttara" (the reply).
But Bṛhaspati says that whoever, having engaged in all manner of conversation, should converse even slightly in secret with another, shall be made to pay the entire amount when accused.
In cases of verbal assault, as well as in disputes over land, one should avoid divine ordeals;
likewise, when there is a connection to the sale or receipt of property, one should avoid ordeal by sacred libation if the defendant is unwilling to undergo it.
If a defendant, when being charged, should attempt to conceal the charge,
one should recognize that as a false plea (*mithyottara*) according to legal procedure. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.3.17)
If, upon hearing the formal charge, the defendant admits it,
that is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be "admission" (saṃpratipatti).
If the defendant, when confronted with a claim by the plaintiff,
admits that very matter and states the grounds for it, that indeed is a plea of counter-claim (pratyavaskandana).
If the defendant admits the very same claim that has been stated by the plaintiff and states the grounds for it,
Manu has declared that the burden of proof lies with the plaintiff.
If one who has fallen away from proper conduct is made to write again, that litigant is considered previously defeated; this is called *prāṅnyāya* (a prior judgment).
One should employ the truth in the case of truth, and one should likewise record falsehood in the case of falsehood;
one should state the grounds in a case supported by grounds, and likewise victory in a case of victory.
That which arises from seeing [something] as fearful is false and is censured by those who know the scriptures;
however, that which is a correct perception is declared to be righteous.
When a legal proceeding is initiated, the truth has been declared by the virtuous as praiseworthy;
that which is contrary would be unrighteous, and the defendant shall suffer defeat.
When the plaintiff and the defendant proceed with mutual rivalry for precedence,
the trial must be conducted according to the order of their castes, while also taking into account the relative gravity of their suffering.
When the defendant has been brought at the same time into the presence of the court members,
he shall then write his reply in accordance with the words of the plaintiff's case.
The rule regarding each specific subject matter has been declared for the purpose of establishing the coherent meaning;
now, that which is to be grasped among the fourfold [means] is being stated.

One should not characterize that which is other than the subject at hand, nor that which is neutral, deficient, excessive, irrelevant, devoid of essential meaning, doubtful, or contrary. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.28)
If he causes fear, or division, or intimidation, or obstruction,
he loses his case in legal proceedings.
But when appointed as an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or the like, both are declared to be equal;
in the sacrifice, the patron obtains merit, while in the debate, he obtains either loss or victory.
When the plaintiff or the defendant dies after the documents have been drawn up in the north-eastern quarter,
their son shall clear up the legal dispute on their behalf.
If a lawsuit remains undecided, the king will be deceived;
the awarding of victory would not be impartial. Therefore, he should decide the cases. (Br̥haspati 1.3.32)
But if one, having designated witnesses,
does not bring them to trial within thirty nights or three fortnights, loss of the case occurs for him.
One who flees when summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the witnesses,
and one who admits his own case— these are the four types of a defeated litigant.
One who flees loses his case after three fortnights; one who remains silent, after seven days;
one whose testimony is contradicted by witnesses, at that very moment; and one who admits the claim, likewise loses it.
Not stating what has been presented, failing to appear,
silence, and the defects of one's own position— these are the characteristics of one who is losing the case.
People know that he who endures being falsely accused in an assembly for a great sin, a minor sin, or a transgression, is endowed with merit.
Therefore, a wise person should diligently perform the purification of the self;
whatever task is most important, that one should first purify.
He who, accused of a great sin, desires to escape from that transgression, deserves punishment for having already admitted it; he is defeated by his own confession.
When a person has made a formal declaration regarding their conduct or a divine ordeal,
but does not present themselves for the trial, one should not allow them to escape by means of a pretext.
If, however, a calamity caused by fate or the king should occur at that time,
he shall not be considered defeated merely by abandoning the ordeal.
When an investigation has been commenced and settled between two parties,
those who subsequently reach a settlement with one another shall be made to pay double the fine.
When the former and latter positions have been set forth and the determination of the case has begun,
there may be a reconciliation between the two heated parties, like that of two pieces of iron.
In that case, there may be a conflict between the witness and the jury;
therefore, the wise should effect a reconciliation between the two while they are still wavering. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.44)
Where there is equality of power between the two, yet a difference in their scriptures and conduct, a peace treaty between both parties is recommended by me for the king. *Bṛhaspati-saṃhitā* 1.3.45.
Where a matter is subject to doubt and the legal procedure is before a king,
a settlement must be made there, just as one joins two pieces of heated iron.
Then peace should be made on equal terms, for an unequal one leads to retreat;
through equality, the king secures dharma, wealth, support, and fame.
Neither witnesses nor jurors suffer distress, and the enemy is turned back.
For men, punishment and favor, the rod, dharma, fame and infamy,
as well as further transgression, all arise from conflict.
Therefore, whatever those who are heads of the family and the assembly, who know the Dharma, who possess impartial vision,
and who are free from hatred and greed may say, that should be done by one who understands.
When the written statement has been properly scrutinized and found to be faultless, then the evidence—
whether from the defendant or the plaintiff— is required as the basis for the legal proceeding. (Br̥hadartha 1.4.1)
But for those who remain in their defense, the members of the court shall investigate;
having properly stated the reply, it must be granted to one of the litigants.
The proponent shall establish his proposition, and likewise the opponent shall establish his grounds;
the proponent shall establish victory by means of the certificate of victory regarding what transpired previously.
Having written down, without omission, the syllables exactly as they appear in the first quarter,
the seeker should establish their meaning through practice in the third quarter.
Having heard the plaintiff's statement,
the members of the court shall direct that he who has made the assertion prove his entire claim by means of written documents and other evidence.
Action is said to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine;
each of these is divided into many types by the seers who know the truth.
Witnesses, documentary evidence, and possession are remembered as the threefold human proof;
while the divine proof is ninefold, beginning with the balance and ending with that born of dharma.
Human proof (mānuṣī kriyā) is threefold: witnesses, documentary evidence, and inference.
Witnesses are recorded as being of twelve types, while documentary evidence is traditionally held to be of eight kinds.
Inference is declared to be threefold, and divine action is ninefold;
in either the first or the third [stage], both divine and human means of proof are authoritative.
In the fourth stage, however, there should be the document of victory along with witnesses;
in matters such as debts and the like, one should employ human means of proof.
In the case of a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or a plea of denial (*pratyavaskanda*), the defendant himself must prove his case;
however, in the case of a plea of falsehood (*mithyottara*), the plaintiff must prove both the matter of the reply and the matter of the original claim.

When witnesses are available, no action is declared to be dependent on fate; and when there is a written document in legal disputes, there should be neither divine ordeals nor witnesses. (Br̥haspati 1.4.12)
In cases of verbal abuse, disputes over land, and even in all four types of violent offenses, divine means of proof are prohibited; nevertheless, they should be employed with great effort.
In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, one should employ divine proof (ordeals).
One who steals heaps of gems, pearls, corals, or necklaces with heart-shaped pendants,
as well as one who is violent and frequents the wives of others, must always be examined by means of oaths.
In cases of accusations of grave crimes, as well as in matters of deposits and their misappropriation,
the king should investigate by means of divine ordeals, even when witnesses are present.
If doubt arises regarding a written document, the testimony of witnesses,
or when an inference is confused, then an ordeal is the means of purification in those cases.
In matters of gambling, duels, and when a legal dispute has arisen, witnesses are declared the sole means of proof; neither divine ordeals nor written documents are required.
The king should cause a decision to be made using whatever witnesses happen to be available; however, in cases of initiated violence, verbal abuse, physical assault,
and matters arising from the use of force, he should rely on witnesses and, indeed, on divine ordeals.

For a debt, documentary evidence, witnesses, or even a trace of circumstantial reasoning, or divine proof (ordeals), has been declared as the means of proof for subjects out of a desire for their welfare. (Br̥haspati 1.4.20)
When witnesses have long since disappeared, when they were made silent long ago, or when inferential evidence has become corrupted,
one should clear the case by means of ordeals.
There should be nine, seven, five, four, or even three witnesses;
or both may be two renowned Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*). One should never question only one person.
The keeper of the gambling hall, the holder of the dice, and likewise one who is present in the midst of the transaction—
each of these alone may be an authority, as may the king and his superintendent.
Thieves, violent criminals, eunuchs, gamblers, and informers are not witnesses because of their wickedness; witness-status is not found among them. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3)
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.1 Witnesses:

The written witness, the secret witness, the reminded witness, the kulya witness, the messenger witness, the incidental witness, the responding witness, and another who is present in the midst of the transaction. Br̥h 1.5.4.
The king, the official, and likewise the village—these are recorded as the twelve kinds of witnesses.
I shall explain their distinctions correctly and in due order.
One by whom his own caste, name, and so forth, as well as those of his father,
and his residence have been recorded, should be known as a witness designated as "written."
When a creditor, having performed transactions such as lending money and so forth with various formal acts,
causes a document to be written in his presence, that is declared to be a "written" (lekhita) document.
But he who is made to hear the statement regarding a debt while separated by a wall,
and who denies it as it actually happened, is called a hidden witness.
He who is summoned and made a witness in matters such as debts, deposits, or transactions, and who is repeatedly reminded, is declared to be a "reminded" witness. [Br̥haspati 1.5.9]
O knower of dharma, one who is related by birth, who is employed in the distribution of shares, in trade, or in service, and who is common to both parties, is proclaimed to be a *kulya*.
But he who, being sent by both parties, listens to the statements of the plaintiff and the defendant,
being virtuous and agreed upon by both, is declared to be a witness (*dūtaka*).
But when a duty is being performed, whoever happens to arrive of his own accord and says,
"I am your witness in this matter," he is called an incidental witness (yādṛcchika).
Where a witness departs for another region or is about to die, one should cause him to declare it to another in due order; that person one should know as a secondary witness (uttarasākṣin).
When witnesses are giving testimony again and again,
he who hears it from hearing after hearing is designated as the "subsequent witness" (uttara-sākṣin).
He upon whom both [parties] have placed their trust and who has been informed of the matter should be known as a secret keeper, having entered into the midst of the business.
Whatever statement has been heard by the king himself from the plaintiff and the defendant,
that alone shall be the witness in case of a disagreement between the two.
But when a legal case has been decided and a new trial should take place, the presiding judge, together with the members of the court, shall be the witness therein; it cannot be otherwise.
Where it has been inhabited and covered on all sides within the boundary, that village is undoubtedly a witness even when it has been cut away. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.18)

Two witnesses who have been written down and likewise kept secret, those written as three, four, or five; those who are summoned by chance, the kulyas, and likewise the secondary witnesses (uttara-sākṣins).
The messenger who holds his own seal, one who is involved in the midst of the business, as well as the king alone and the presiding official—these shall be the authorities. (Br̥haspati Smr̥ti 1.5.20)
But the plaintiff who, by means of a fault, seeks to corrupt witnesses who have been duly designated for the case—
corrupting those who are faultless— deserves a fine equal to the value of the suit. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21)
Whatever defects of a written document exist, as well as those attributed to witnesses, must be stated at the time of the trial; one should not raise them after they have already been spoken.
The defendant must set forth the defects of the witnesses in court;
having written all of them down on a document, he should then state his answer.
They are never entitled to act as witnesses regarding the performance [of a rite];
therefore, they must be meditated upon otherwise by the defendant during the ritual action.
If the defendant does not clearly establish his defense by means of witnesses, he must be compelled to pay;
likewise, all witnesses who have been examined but fail to uphold the duty of a witness are to be excluded.
Whether it be the defendant or the plaintiff, when proving a defect in a witness,
there shall be no separate legal proceeding, provided it is relevant to the matter at hand.

If the plaintiff has no further desire [to contest the case] and the witness remains established in the truth, he who has been defeated shall be made to pay a fine according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
But he who, after witnesses have been declared, disparages those previously unimpeached and does not state the grounds for that [disparagement], shall incur the first amercement.
In a legal dispute, if either the documents or the witnesses are found to be tainted,
the case of that party shall not be adjudicated until those [tainted elements] have been cleared.
But when a verdict has been reached by the witnesses and the members of the court having spoken, if anyone should initiate a renewed dispute, the king shall investigate that case himself.
When witnesses are suspected of corruption, the purification of the witnesses must first be carried out;
once the witnesses have been cleared, one may thereafter purify the case itself. (Br̥haspati 1.5.31)
The members of the assembly, who are conversant with the meaning of the treatises on Dharma, must admonish them with words praising truth and by means of rejecting falsehood.
Whatever merit you have earned from birth until death—
all that goes to ruin through the false accusation of a lie.
A false witness, a false accuser, and a slayer of a Brahmin are declared to be equal;
a destroyer of an embryo and a betrayer of a friend are said to be no greater than these.
Having understood this, the witness who speaks according to the truth thereby attains fame in this world and a blessed state in the next.
There are men who, out of greed, would state a legal matter otherwise;
and there are others, evil-minded men, who forge false documents.
I shall now describe those witnesses who are to be questioned, as well as those lowest of men who are to be excluded, as prescribed by the scriptures.
Those engaged in the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, free from greed and hatred,
of noble birth, irreproachable, and endowed with austerity, charity, and compassion, are witnesses.
The father of the mother, the paternal uncle, the wife’s brother and mother,
the brother, the friend, and the son-in-law are not witnesses in any legal disputes.
Those addicted to other men's wives or to drinking, gamblers, those previously convicted,
the insane, the afflicted, the reckless, and atheists are not eligible as witnesses.
Even virtuous persons would not be valid witnesses if the wealthy man has died,
provided they were merely informed by the son after the dying man himself had been near death.
Having removed his sandals and turban, he should raise his right hand;
taking gold, cow-dung, and darbha grass, he should speak the truth.
Those who present themselves [as refugees] should be examined by means of their voice, complexion, gestures, and so forth.

Even if one must speak untruths, one should protect a Brahmin who has committed an offense through a single lapse, one who is afflicted by calamity, or one who is being executed by soldiers and the like.
He whose entire claim has been corroborated by witnesses shall be the victor; otherwise, however, he shall not attain his objective.
If a witness who is free from disease does not come when summoned,
he shall be made to pay both the debt and a fine after three fortnights have passed.
In a conflict between witnesses, those who are numerous should be accepted; if they are equal in number, those endowed with good qualities;
if there is a conflict between those with good qualities, those engaged in virtuous action; and if they are equal in that regard, those who are more pure.
Witnesses who, when not questioned, fail to speak the truth, or likewise do not answer a question when asked, should be restrained, censured, and punished according to the law.
If that which is spoken is not deficient in terms of place, time, age, substance, name, caste, and measure, one should declare the object to be accomplished as achieved.
In cases where there may be disagreement regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, form, or caste,
that testimony as well must not be otherwise [i.e., it must be accepted].
If a witness, when questioned regarding the matters specified, does not speak when the time for testimony has arrived, that is equal to the loss of his senses; it is not considered a valid statement.
One should contemplate the entirety of what was proposed in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa);
however, that which was stated there as deficient or excessive shall not be considered as having been truly declared.
Where witnesses state a matter either deficiently or excessively, that matter should be understood as not having been stated; this is remembered as the rule regarding witnesses.
When the portion of the matter to be proven has been declared by the witnesses, it shall be considered as fully established;
this applies to matters involving sexual intercourse, violent acts, and theft, which are determined by what is proven.
Wherever there may be a deficiency or an excess in testimony, one should reject that testimony;
in such a case, the witness should not be punished, for he deserves punishment for failing to speak.
This determination regarding the number and characteristics of witnesses has been declared;
now I shall state the rules for written documents in their proper order. (Bṛhaspati 1.6.1)
Since confusion may arise even regarding matters such as debts and the like,
the Creator created letters and placed them upon paper in ancient times.

[Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.1: Characteristics of a Written Document] A document is said to be that which records local custom, the amount paid as interest, the increase in years, months, fortnights, and so forth, and is marked with the signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe. Br̥h 1.6.3.
A royal edict, one executed by a local official, and likewise one written in one's own hand—
documentary evidence is declared to be of these three kinds; furthermore, it is divided into many varieties.
Secular documents are of seven kinds— arising from shares, gifts, purchases, pledges, agreements, slaves, and debts— and royal edicts are of three kinds.
This document known as the *vibhāgapatra* (partition deed) is executed for the determination of shares;
when a boundary dispute has been settled, it is traditionally called a *sīmāpatra* (boundary deed).
A deed of gift, a deed of partition, and likewise a deed concerning boundaries;
a deed of purchase, a deed concerning a slave, and thereafter a deed of mortgage.
A document of mutual agreement, a deed of victory,
and likewise a treaty— these are of many kinds according to the differences in their legal transactions.
A pledge-deed shall be for the purpose of a pledge; a slave-document shall be for the purpose of a slave.
For the sake of accomplishing their desired aims, the village councils, guilds,
and assemblies have executed this deed-of-pledge (saṃvittipatra) for the purpose of dharma, in accordance with the scriptures.
When brothers who have divided their inheritance among themselves by mutual consent execute a document of partition, that is called a *bhāgalekhya* (a deed of partition).
But that which one should make into a document after giving land, valid for as long as the moon and sun endure—
an unseizable and irremovable deed of gift— that indeed they know to be a *dānalekhya*.

When, having purchased a house, field, or the like, one causes a document to be executed that includes the equivalent price and the names [of the parties], that is called a *krayalekhya* (purchase deed). (Br̥haspati 1.6.13)
When one executes a document after giving movable or immovable property as a pledge,
provided it is associated with the conditions of being kept in custody or being used, that is known as a *ādhi-lekhya* (mortgage deed).
Whatever a village or a district may do for one another in a state of intoxication,
provided it does not conflict with the king and is for the sake of dharma or wealth, they call that a "contract-deed" (saṃvitpatra).
Whatever work one who is destitute of clothing and food performs in the wilderness, "I shall do that work for you"—this is considered a contract of servitude (dāsapatra). Br̥haspati 1.6.16.
Having received wealth through interest, one may either perform the transaction oneself or cause it to be done by another;
this is declared by the wise to be a *uddhāra-patra*, a document of debt.
Regarding the established status of guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like that has been proclaimed, its proof is documentary evidence; neither divine ordeals nor witnesses are required.

However, for the sake of maintaining the agreement of guilds, corporations, and the like, that which is established is called a *sthitipatra* (deed of settlement) by those who know the *smṛtis* of Manu and others. (Br̥haspati 1.6.19)

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.3: The King’s Edict on Gifts] Having bestowed land and other gifts, the king shall cause a charter to be made upon a copper plate or a cloth, containing the law and joined with the place, lineage, and other particulars. Br̥h 1.6.20.
For the merit of my parents and myself,
I have today given this gift to such-and-such a fellow practitioner for the sake of such-and-such a son.
Inviolable and unseizable, it is entirely free from all that is to be cultivated;
it lasts as long as the moon and sun, and follows one's lineage of sons and grandsons.

One should record that for sixty thousand years, the fruit of obstructing a gift belongs to the one who cuts off the giving, while heaven is for the giver and protector, and hell indeed for the one who takes it away.
"The ocean, the rains, the months, and so forth, along with the figures for the treasury—
these have been ascertained by me," thus it was written by the scribes of peace and war.
Such a royal edict is declared to be one "written by favor" (prasādalikhita),
which the king issues after having inscribed the name of the recipient and other details.
Indeed, that which is written by way of favor when the king is pleased by service, valor, and so forth, is a *jayapatra* (document of victory);
it is issued at the conclusion of the determination of the plaint and the reply, and the arguments regarding the proceedings.
One should grant a document to the victor; that is called a "document of victory" (jayapatra).

Whatever occurred in the legal proceeding— the plaint, the reply, and so forth— along with the evidence and the final determination, he shall write all of that in the document of victory (*jayapatra*).
One should establish the matter to be proved in a victory that is endowed with the four components;
indeed, a document of victory (jayapatra) is required to be accompanied by the royal seal.
To others who are devoid of other means of proof and so forth, [the truth] is granted;
and that which is established through the restatement of the facts shall be the document of victory (jayapatra).
A document executed by one who is about to die, by those whose property has been diminished or lost, by those afflicted by madness or calamity,
or by force of poison or fraud, is not valid.
Where a single witness who is tainted or censurable is appointed,
that is declared to be a forged document, as is the case with a scribe of similar character.
A document that is brilliant yet old, soiled though recent,
broken, or composed of indistinct syllables, shall be considered forged.
Just as a reflection situated in a mirror appears to exist though it is non-existent,
so too do skillful people create painted images that possess the likeness of forms.
For a judgment is indeed based on truth, while a refutation is based solely on fault;
that court where such a corrupted proceeding is deliberated is truly a royal assembly.
Having deliberated together with the Brahmins, one should examine the fault of the speaker.
By that [evidence] through which witnesses, scribes, or executors fall into falsehood, by that the document shall be deemed corrupt; one should declare it pure when the parties are pure.
If a debtor denies a debt that has been entered in writing with his own hand,
he may be compelled by means of witnesses recorded in the document, by oral testimony, or by the testimony of the scribe.

But when letters are displaced from their positions, lack beauty, are indistinct, or have fallen away from their defining characteristics— wherever such [letters] may stand, Bhṛgu says that the writing is then defective.
The plaintiff shall clear up the documentary evidence, but his son shall clear up the possession alone;
if he has died while being sued, his son shall clear up that [possession].
Having ascertained the matter, those skilled in place and time who forge documents produce a corresponding written record; one should examine that with great care.
Some skillful people write [the letters] like a painting;
therefore, it is held that perfection does not result solely from the power of writing.

One's own relatives may deceive women, children, the afflicted, or those ignorant of writing by having them sign a document marked with their own names; such a deed must be scrutinized through reasoning and legal precedents.
When an error occurs in this threefold document,
one should then correct it by the hand-signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.

One should recognize that where a fraudulent pretext (*upadhi*) has been employed, there is "exertion" (*udyāma*) due to the undertaking of the enterprise, "acquisition" (*ādhāna*) due to the gathering of the fruit, and "abundance of wealth" (*dhanāḍhyatva*) due to the presence of the counter-party. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.44)
A document is established as valid in all cases— provided it was shown at the proper time, read aloud, and made known— if so, it remains effective even when the witnesses have died.
Where the expressive power of syllables is obstructed by speakers,
there would be a total destruction of actions and an infinite regress would arise.
A document that is more than thirty years old, and which has neither been seen nor heard of,
does not attain validity, even if witnesses are still living.
But when a peaceful settlement has been reached, if the defendant does not produce the written document and the debtor does not demand it, he shall incur doubt regarding the matter.

One should cause the members of families, guilds, assemblies, and so forth to hear and remember [the law] as it has been presented at the appropriate time; in this way, it shall become more authoritative.
If anything has been received, or if there is a formal designation [of the debt],
that very document shall serve as proof, even if the witnesses have died.
If one who is capable does not request a debt from a wealthy person standing nearby,
out of a suspicion that he might be cleared of the obligation, the written document in that case shall be rendered weak in its evidentiary force.
A document executed by those who are insane, dull-witted, or women; by those fleeing from fear of the king; or by those who are timid, frightened, or afflicted, shall not be subject to invalidation.
Then, when the scribe has met his death along with the witnesses,
there is no doubt that [the matter] is purified by their own handwriting and other such evidence.
When there is doubt regarding a debt, whether the debtor is living or deceased,
the determination of that document is made by other documents written in his own hand.
When doubt arises regarding a document, if the witnesses, the scribe,
and the author are found to be corrupt, [the authenticity of the document] should be determined by means of previous letters written in their own hands and other such evidence.
A written document is never set aside by witnesses or by an oath; however, one suffers loss through neglect by failing to produce it or by failing to have it read aloud.
Therefore, both of these must be examined especially by the king;
there should be only one document for the sake of establishing a single matter.
However, among many types of documents, one may produce a defect:

that which is contrary to local custom, ambiguous, devoid of proper sequence, executed by one who is not the owner, or lacking a valid point of contention—such a document is defective. (Br̥haspati 1.6.58)
All activities have wealth as their root, and all efforts are considered to be for its attainment;
its prescribed method consists of increasing it, protecting it, and enjoying it. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.7.1)
Furthermore, that is to be known as threefold: the white, the variegated, and the black;
therein, the classification is further to be understood as sevenfold.

Wealth acquired through learning, heroism, austerity, a daughter, a pupil, a sacrificer, or inheritance—these are the seven kinds of wealth; for both [the teacher and the pupil] are entitled to such wealth.
That which is obtained through idleness, agriculture, trade, tolls, the practice of crafts,
or from one who has rendered assistance, is declared to be variegated (śabala).
That which is acquired through gambling with dice and the like, by means of messengers, by counterfeiting, through acts of violence, or under some pretext, is declared to be "black" wealth.
By means of that, buying and selling, giving and receiving,
as well as various activities and the enjoyment of possessions, are carried out.
Whatever a person performs with a particular kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit of that action both after death and in this world.
Furthermore, that [meditation] is known to be twelvefold, based on the individual castes;
it is threefold as common, and the remainder is known to be ninefold.
That which is inherited by lineage, that which is received as a gift of affection, and that which is acquired together with one's wife—
these three types of property are declared to belong to all social classes (varṇas) without distinction.

The specific wealth of a Brahmin should be known as having three characteristics: that which is obtained through acceptance of gifts, that which is earned from officiating at sacrifices, and likewise that which is received from a pupil. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.7.10.
They say that the specific wealth of a Kṣatriya is also threefold: that acquired through battle, from taxes, and from fines levied in legal proceedings.
The specific wealth of a Vaiśya should also be known as having three characteristics:
agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade; and for a Śūdra, [his duty is] service to these [other classes].
For all social classes alike, the acquisition of wealth in this manner is righteous;
otherwise, it would be unrighteous, unless there is a grave emergency.

In times of distress, the performance of the Vaiśya's livelihood is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa as the next best alternative; however, a lower livelihood is never permitted for him under any circumstances.
A Brahmin should never perform the work of a Śūdra, nor should a Śūdra perform the work of a Brahmin; for those two acts lead to the downfall of each respectively.
Between those two, no superior or inferior action exists;
for, having set aside intermediate actions, they are indeed common to all.

Having crossed over a time of distress, when his people have been supported by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa should relinquish that Kṣatriya occupation after performing a purificatory rite for himself.
But that Brahmin who, out of sensual passion, delights in that very act of eating is called a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*; he has fallen from the path and is thus designated as one marked [with disgrace].
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes to the family of another,
is known as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* because of that misconduct.
When the performance of legal business has been carried out by daylight in villages and cities,
and when witnesses are available, divine proof (ordeals) is not to be employed.
Likewise, in matters such as the use of doors, paths, water conduits, and so forth, the mere fact of enjoyment by the superior party shall suffice;
there is no need for a document nor witnesses.
This rule regarding witnesses and written documents has been declared;
now the law concerning the acquisition of immovable property and possession is being stated.

Immovable property acquired through learning, purchase, alliance, valor, inheritance, or family tradition, as well as the share of a sapinda who is childless, may be taken by force even from one who possesses it. (Bṛhaspati 1.7.23)
Regarding the sevenfold enjoyment:

"In the paternal estate, enjoyment consisting of what is obtained through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, valor, and discovery—when this sevenfold enjoyment is acquired along with its legal title, it attains validity. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.7.24)
That possession which has come down by succession, is authorized by the scriptures, and is accompanied by purchase or formal transfer—
such a possession indeed attains validity.
Immovable property acquired through partition, purchase, inheritance from a father, or received from the king attains validity by being enjoyed; it is lost through neglect.
If a person's possession has begun with formal occupation and has continued for thirty years without interruption or legal challenge, one shall not displace him from that possession.
There shall be no enjoyment of women by any means whatsoever without a written document;
nor [may there be enjoyment] of the wealth of the king, of a Śrotriya, or of the property of the mentally disabled or of minors.
One cannot attain perfection through possession alone;
nor can one attain it through pure scriptural authority alone. It is attained through both, and not otherwise.
