When the wealth of a learned Śrotriya or that obtained from a father in due succession has been acquired,
neither the one who took it nor his son should exert force regarding its enjoyment.
The law is established as follows: if, within a single legal document, cattle, women, men, and so forth, as well as villages, fields, and groves, are recorded; [then it is valid]. (Br̥haspati 1.7.32)
Even when only a portion is enjoyed, all [the owners] are considered to have been deprived of their property;
for title alone has no force where there is not even a slight amount of possession.
An eyewitness is superior to inference; a written document is weightier than eyewitnesses;
and possession by three successive generations, being unimpeded, is more authoritative than these.
Inference resides here, and the witness [of possession] shall exist until death;
however, a document and possession that are uncontradicted are authoritative for three generations.
If one’s father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are all living,
yet land has been enjoyed for thirty years without being obstructed by others, [that possession is valid].
That possession is to be known as *pauruṣī*; that which is double is *dvipuruṣī*;
that which is triple is *tripūruṣī*; and beyond that, it is considered *cirantanā* (of long standing).
Where the defendant is accused, the document is more authoritative than the witness;
in the absence of those, possession alone is the most weighty proof among the sons.
The one who brings forth [the claim] should establish possession or the title in an assembly;
his son may establish possession alone; but a grandson or later descendant may establish nothing at all. (Br̥haspati 1.7.39)
If property is given openly by others to one who is the heir,
yet another person subsequently enjoys it, that first person is not entitled to recover it.
He who, seeing another giving away land, does not restrain him,
shall not regain that land even by means of a valid document.
Bhṛgu says that what is given by the heirs or by others belongs to that very person.
The enjoyment [of property] by three generations shall be established for others; there is no doubt in this matter.
As long as the sapinda relationship has not ceased, it is not established for the sakulyas.
But that which has been enjoyed by one who is not the owner— such as a house, field, or shop—
does not become lost to the friend, kinsman, or relative through such enjoyment.
The dharma of a learned Vedic scholar is imperishable; he has no fear from royal officials;
he possesses affection for friends and kinsmen; and what he has eaten is never lost.
That which has been eaten by those related by marriage, by Vedic scholars (śrotriya), and likewise by kings and ministers,
does not bear fruit for them even after a very long period of time.

If land that has been recorded in a royal edict is enjoyed by another person, it is not lost through such enjoyment in the case of those who are powerless, lazy, afflicted by disease, children, fearful, or travelers.
When a house or field has been deprived of its enjoyment, and doubt arises therein,
one should establish its purity through a document, those who know of the possession, or witnesses.

Those who know the names of the parties, the document, the number, the time, the direction and location, as well as the cause for the enjoyment or the termination [of the property], are the witnesses in that case.
Those who have been born very recently, as well as those residing in other lands, are designated as the primary witnesses; they should be questioned in the determination of the legal matter.
But what those who are free from malice and impartial in their view should declare regarding a doubtful matter, that must be accepted as authoritative; in this way, dharma is not lost.
That which has been declared regarding immovable property serves to establish ownership and enjoyment;
however, in a dispute concerning a claim lacking proof, the divine means of proof (divya) should be prescribed.
Even if it was enjoyed by three preceding kings without formal title,
a royal grant of land must never be confiscated from him by a king at any time.
Where possession has been exercised by three generations and is now extended into the fourth, that enjoyment attains stability; one need not inquire about the title of acquisition in such a case.
But when something has been enjoyed by three generations of men and was not prohibited, no legal title need be produced; in that case, possession is the weightier factor.
In disputes concerning immovable property, possession extending over three generations is to be known as independent; it is the authoritative means for determining the matter to be proved.
If the enjoyment [of land] by three generations is accompanied by a formal document,
such a gift to a Brahmin (brahmadeya) cannot be taken away.
If possession has been held by three generations in a continuous line of succession,
it cannot be overturned except by a prior royal edict.
If land has been enjoyed for three generations in the presence of the owner without protest,
it must not be taken away from him, unless he declares that he possesses a title of ownership.
In the legal treatises, possession that is long-standing and uninterrupted is indeed powerful;
however, even that which has been interrupted is to be recognized as valid if it was previously established.

Whatever property was enjoyed by the father according to custom and in accordance with dharma, even when he has passed away, that is acquired by the son through such enjoyment; it belongs to him by virtue of that enjoyment.
But when land has been enjoyed by three persons in due order according to the law,
a fourth person may acquire it there even in the absence of a written document.

Whatever has been enjoyed by kinsmen of the same lineage, by relatives, and likewise by one's own people—there is no attainment [of merit] from such enjoyment; one should instead direct the enjoyment toward others.
Possession is fivefold: it consists of title, long duration, absence of interruption or opposition, the presence of the adversary, and actual enjoyment. (Br̥haspati Sm̐rti 1.7.64)
One will suffer loss of quadrupeds, wealth, grain, and so forth, within a year.
Non-enjoyment of land, failure to produce a document at the proper time,
and the failure to recall witnesses— these indeed cause the loss of one's own right.
Therefore, one should diligently maintain the authority of the means of valid cognition;
by that, all matters, both stationary and moving, are accomplished.
In a case that occurred long ago and lacks witnesses, one should question the subsequent witnesses,
or subject the defendant to oaths, or employ an ordeal.
And there is the absence of obstruction in teaching, as well as a portion of the method of reasoning.
That which has been stolen by thieves must be recovered from all [suspects] and restored;
if it cannot be found, it must be paid from his own treasury. Failing to do so, he would incur the guilt of a thief.
Thus has been declared the means for attaining profit and enjoyment regarding immovable property.
In a lawsuit lacking legal proof, however, divine evidence is considered faultless. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.8.1)
When the inferential means of proof are corrupted, one should purify the matter by divine methods;
the divine ordeal is recorded as being of nine kinds, beginning with the balance and ending with the *dharmaja* (the sacred libation).
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth is the sacred libation (kośa);
the sixth is said to be rice grains, and the seventh is the heated gold bean (taptamāṣaka).
The eighth is said to be the time (kāla), and likewise the ninth is the dharma;
all these have been declared by the Self-Existent One as they come through divine means.
[The Divine Arrangement] Since these have been employed by the high-souled gods for the sake of difficult matters,
I shall state them in their general outlines for the sake of clarifying doubtful points.
These are employed in their proper sequence according to place, time, purpose, and number.
According to the sequence of offenses and with the intention of declaring what is right or wrong,
these [penances] must be administered according to the rule prescribed in the scriptures, and not otherwise.
In matters such as debts and the like, when there is a mutual disagreement,
the witnesses should be made to provide testimony accompanied by details regarding the quantity of the property and likewise considering the status of the individuals involved.
For the sake of worldly transaction, this designation has been declared on earth:
a coin made from a karṣa of copper is to be known as a kārṣika paṇa.
Four *niṣkas* of gold are one *kārṣika*; a *paṇa* is made of copper.
A coin struck from a *karṣa* of copper should be known as a *kārṣika-paṇa*.
That same [weight] is called an *āndrikā*, and four of those are a *dhānakā*.
Twelve of those are a *suvarṇa*, which is also known as a *dīnāra*.
A fine of one thousand kārṣāpaṇas is the highest amercement;
half of that is declared the middle, and half of that is recorded as the lowest.
The balance should be administered to a Brāhmaṇa, fire to a Kṣatriya, water should be given to a Vaiśya, and poison alone to a Śūdra. (Bṛhaspati 1.8.12)
The treasury of all is declared by the wise to be common to them all.
Witnesses may fall into disagreement due to affection, anger, or greed;
however, no disagreement ever arises regarding a divine ordeal administered according to the prescribed rule.
The divine ordeal should be administered according to the prescribed rule by those expert in divine matters;
if it is administered contrary to what has been stated, then neither the proof nor the disproof is established.
Gifts given at an improper place or time, or those performed outside of the prescribed ritual boundaries, undoubtedly cause failure regarding one's goals in this world; of this there is no doubt.
The ordeal must be administered to the accused by those experts in ordeals;
either one may perform it according to his own preference, while the other shall undergo the cutting of the head.
One may administer the ordeal even without a formal charge in cases of treason against the king or mortal sin;
the administration of divine ordeals is declared [to apply] elsewhere except by royal command.
No one should thus subject an accuser to divine ordeals.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa— these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.2) p.83 [Celestial Deities] Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.19.
Between Deveśa and Īśāna is the path of the Ādityas;
namely Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth;
after him Tvaṣṭṛ, and then Viṣṇu, who is not the youngest, though born of the youngest.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names.
To the western part of Agni, they know to be the abode of the Rudras:
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, and the highly illustrious Girīśa.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aprajita; Brh_1.8.23.
Bhuvanādhiśvara, Kapālī the lord of the people,
Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhaga— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
Between the Lord of the Dead (Yama) and the Rākṣasa, one should arrange the station of the Mothers:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā accompanied by her attendants;
they know the abode of Gaṇeśa to be in the northern part of Nirṛti.
In the northern region of Varuṇa, the abode of the Maruts is said to be located;
[the names of the wind-gods are] Śvasana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, and likewise Māruta.
[Regarding divine matters by means of the number of substances:
The number of rays, rooted in goats, was proclaimed by Manu;
that [scale] ending with the kārṣāpaṇa should be employed in divine [ordeals], and one should administer them accordingly. Br̥h. 1.8.28.
When a thousand *paṇas* have been stolen, poison is the ordeal;

when three-quarters [of a thousand] have been stolen, fire; when two-quarters [of a thousand] have been stolen, water; and when half [of a thousand] have been stolen, the balance should always be administered.
In a lawsuit involving four hundred [paṇas], the ordeal of the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka) must be administered;
for three hundred, rice grains (taṇḍula) should be given; and for half of that, the ordeal of the sacred water (kośa) should be used.
When a hundred [coins] have been lost or stolen, a purification by means of dharma must be administered;
the members of the court should diligently apply the plough-test to the one accused of stealing the cattle.
Or, upon the destruction of half a *yava*, there is the destruction of its half-measure of rice;
and when half of that, and then half of that again, have been destroyed, worldly activity (*laukikī kriyā*) is considered appropriate.

The vehicles and weapons of the virtuous, cattle, seeds, and gold; the feet of the gods and Brahmins; and the heads of one's sons and wife—[these are the objects of oath-taking]. (Bṛhad-āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.4; Śapathavidhi 1.8.33)
These oaths have been declared as always easy to perform for minor matters;
however, for violent acts and grave accusations, they say that divine ordeals are the means of purification.

One should say "Speak! to a Brāhmaṇa; "Speak the truth! to a Kṣatriya; [threaten] a Vaiśya with the loss of his cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra with all possible sins. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.35)
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by [the truth of] the Vedas; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons;
cowherds, merchants, artisans, and actors, by their cattle; servants and usurers, by their wealth; and one should treat Brahmins [of these latter classes] as Śūdras. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.8.36)
Even those who have strayed from their own duties and subsist on the alms of others,
yet desire the status of the twice-born— one should treat them as Śūdras.
Each person should be made to swear an oath corresponding to their social class.
There is no sin in [lying] regarding women, marriages, cattle, fuel, the protection of Brahmins, or in taking an oath. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.8.39)
Witnesses must give their testimony within the assembly and not elsewhere;
for this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in matters concerning immovable property.
If the death of living beings is involved, one should cause the testimony to be declared in the presence of the corpse;
in its absence, however, in the presence of identifying marks, but never otherwise.
Witnesses who have arrived at the place of dispute must not, even with great effort, speak the truth unless they are questioned or appointed to do so.
The testimony of those witnesses, which is stated spontaneously and free from defects, is to be accepted;
once it has been spoken, the witnesses should not be questioned again and again by the king.
For witnesses, members of the court, and those who have fallen from their status, there is no rule for returning to their former state.
Then the seven seers, Indra, and the others, whose wealth was their asceticism,
made an oath at Puṣkara with undistracted minds for the sake of mutual purification.
Within seven days, or within two weeks, no misfortune arising from kings or divine causes shall occur;
he remains pure regarding his kinsmen, sapinda relatives, and wealth through oaths.
In the absence of any human evidence whatsoever, the decision must be made by divine means alone;
however, when witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid recourse to divine proof.
Thus, the number for those of inferior quality is established; for those of middling quality, it is remembered as double that;
but for those of superior quality, it should be calculated as fourfold by the investigators.
[The Procedure for the Balance] [p.87] When the accused is weighed on the balance, if he is lighter, he shall suffer loss;
if he is equal, he shall be weighed again; if he is heavier, he shall be the victor. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.5) [Note: This verse is numbered as 1.8.49 in some editions.]
In the event of the breaking of the sling or the snapping of the axle, the king shall provide a new sling;
the witnesses should be excellent Brahmins who speak according to what they have actually seen.
The king should appoint kinsmen who are pure and free from greed;
the determination of purity or impurity must be understood according to their testimony. (Bṛhaspati 1.8.51)
In the event of the cutting of the armpit-cloth, the breaking of the balance-beam, or likewise the breaking of the *dhaṭa* or the *karkaṭa*,
as well as the snapping of the cord or the breaking of the axle, one shall incur impurity in exactly the same way.
[The Ritual for the Fire (Agnividhi):
I shall proclaim the ritual for the fire exactly as it is enjoined by the injunctions.
One should cause eight mandalas to be made, and likewise a ninth one in front. Brh_1,8.53.
The first mandala is that of Agni; the second is known as that of Varuṇa;
the third has Vāyu as its presiding deity, and the fourth has Yama as its presiding deity.
The fifth, however, has Indra as its deity; the sixth is said to belong to Kubera;
the seventh has Soma as its deity; and the eighth has all the gods [or the Sun] as its deity.
That which is the ninth, situated before it, they know to be the Great Earth;
it should be made of cow-dung and moistened with water that has stood overnight.
They say that the space between one mandala and another is thirty-two finger-breadths;
however, the mandala should be made according to the measure of the performer's own even step.
Then another man of similar appearance, taking up a middle-sized arrow,
should return with speed from the direction where that first man had gone.
But when the arrow-retriever, having entered the water, does not clearly see [the object] within the water,
then one should declare him pure.
When the middle arrow has been brought back, one whose body was pierced by it shall attain purity;
otherwise, one would not be purified even upon the sight of a single limb [of the victim],
whether due to remaining in that place or moving elsewhere, in whichever spot one first deposited the arrow.
Having cast the man into the waters, one should discharge three arrows;
however, a wise man should not shoot them when a strong wind from the Maruts is blowing. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.62.
And on uneven ground, crowded with trees and stumps, and filled with grass, shrubs, creepers, vines, mud, and stones. [Br̥had-yogiyājñavalkya-smṛti 1.8.63]

He by whom poison administered according to the prescribed rite has been digested without the use of mantras or medicine shall be deemed pure; otherwise, however, he shall be punished and made to pay that wealth.
He whose loss of sons, wife, or wealth does not occur within seven days or fourteen days shall be pure; of this there is no doubt.
[The Procedure for the Vessel (Kośavidhi):
Whatever food the accused has eaten, that itself shall be the circle of weapons.
Having washed it, one should make him drink three handfuls of that water. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.8.66)
The king should cause a restricted area to be patrolled there for three or five nights by his own men, out of suspicion of tricksters.

In cases of a great accusation, in matters lacking righteousness, against one who is ungrateful, a coward, or contemptible, against an atheist, and against one whose guilt has been witnessed, one should reject the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośa-pāna).
One should always avoid divine [medicines] for men afflicted by diseases; however,
one should not employ rice-grains for those among the people suffering from diseases of the mouth.
Fasting during a solar eclipse, one who is pure should eat rice grains;
he becomes purified by vomiting white [rice], but if the opposite occurs, he incurs fault. (Br̥had-yogiyājñavalkya 1.8.70)
Where blood is seen, and the jaw and palate fail,
and whose body trembles— one should designate such a person as impure.
Free from fear, one should extract a heated bean from well-heated oil or ghee by joining the thumb and finger, while invoking the truth. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.10; 1.8.72)
Having taken cow's ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay, one who is pure should heat it over a fire.
One should cast into it a very beautiful ring made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, having washed it once with water.
In that place rich with swirling waves of heroic power, which is beyond the reach of touch by the nails,
one should examine the sacrificial pap (caru) with a fresh leaf to see if it makes a sound.
Then, with this mantra, he should consecrate it once:
"O ghee, you are the supreme purifier, the nectar among sacrificial rites. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.76)
O purifier, burn away his evil; O cool one as snow, become pure!
Then, when he has fasted, bathed, and arrived wearing wet clothes—
One should likewise cause that seal-ring to be placed in the midst of clarified butter.
Then the examiners should examine her ring finger;
if she can shake the tip of her hand without a blister appearing,
she is pure according to the law, just as the word of the Grandfather [Brahmā] declares.
[A procedure for the plowshare:
An iron plowshare weighing twelve palas, when heated, is called a *phāla*.
If it remains unburnt, one attains purification; otherwise, however, one is disgraced. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.11; 1.8.79)
It should be eight finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide;
glowing like fire, the thief should lick it once with his tongue.
If he is not burned, he attains purification; otherwise, he is defeated.
In major charges, the members of the court must diligently provide the ploughshare for the defendant when the accuser has placed his head upon it. Br̥haspati 1.8.81.
[The Ritual for Distinguishing Dharma and Adharma:
Dharma and adharma, white and black respectively, should be written upon two leaves with mantras such as those for the gift of life, and with Sāman chants beginning with the Gāyatrī. Brh_1,8.82.
Having addressed [the image], one should worship it with perfumes and white and black flowers;
then, having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the two [images] should be enclosed within lumps of clay.
Having made those two equal, they should be placed in a jar unobserved;
then, one should take a single lump from the jar without delay.
When the law is upheld, he shall be pure and worthy of honor by those who investigate; but when unrighteousness is upheld, he should be punished or even banished. [p.93] Brh_1.8.85.
One should draw dharma and adharma as white and black respectively upon a birch-bark leaf;
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship it with perfumes and garlands.
Dharma is white-flowered, while adharma is the wearer of black flowers;
having prepared them in this manner and smeared them, one should place those [flowers] upon the two lumps.
Then, two equal-sized balls should be made either from cow dung or from clay;
they should be placed in an undamaged earthen vessel and remain unobserved.
In a clean place that has been smeared [with cow dung], in the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
he should then worship the gods and the world-protectors (lokapālas) as before.
Preceded by the invocation of Dharma, one should write a written pledge:
"If I am free from sin, may Dharma come into my hand. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.8.90)
When accused, he should take one of the two without delay;
if he takes the dharma, he shall be purified, but if he takes the adharma, he is defeated.
Reflecting in this manner, the king does not fall away from dharma or artha.

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.9. The Method of Decision] "In a matter that is doubtful, a decision is declared to be of four kinds: by means of dharma, by legal procedure, by conduct, and by the king's command. (Br̥h 1.9.1)
Each one of these has been declared by the wise to be of two kinds according to the difference in action;
and one should determine the punishment in accordance with the offense.
Having properly deliberated upon the matter and determined it through reasoning,
and having examined it by means of oaths— that is to be known as a legal decision according to Dharma.
Where the defendant admits [the claim], that is a legal decision;
a decision thoroughly purified by ordeals is declared to be a correct one.
That discourse which is established by means of valid cognition is called the first; the second is proclaimed as that which lacks a response to quibbles (*vākchala*). *Bṛhatī* 1.9.5.
Conduct determined by inference is so described;
however, the third [type] is cited by those learned in the scriptures as being based on local custom.

But when there is equality of the means of proof, the king’s command is declared the final decision; this is proclaimed as the fourth case, provided it does not contradict the scriptures or the members of the court. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.9.7)
But when there is a conflict with the Dharmaśāstras, a rule that is consistent with reason is remembered as authoritative.
Except for killing, there is never a punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
Brāhmaṇas and cows are not to be slain—this is the Vedic tradition in this world.
Even if he is guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), a Brahmin does not deserve corporal punishment;
rather, the king should impose banishment, branding, and shaving of the head upon him.
And those who have committed great offenses, he should punish with the penalty of death.

For a very slight offense, there shall be punishment by word or the "fie" reprimand; for the first degree of violence, the same applies; but for the middle and highest degrees, the punishment shall be half of that [prescribed for the highest], and for treason against the king, imprisonment.
One who desires his own welfare should either banish or even execute those who have committed a great sin (mahāpātaka), whether individually or all together. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.9.13.

One should employ verbal punishment against friends and others, saying, "Shame on you, wretched men! And one should punish with fines those men who are quarrelsome or hostile. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.9.14)

Neither father, nor teacher, nor friend, nor mother, nor wife, nor son, nor domestic priest—there is no one who, having deviated from his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.9.15)
Sacrificial priests, domestic chaplains, ministers, sons, kinsmen,
and relatives who have deviated from dharma should be punished by kings or banished from the city.
One should punish gurus, domestic priests, and those worthy of honor solely with the punishment of speech;
other disputants, however, one should punish with reproach and fines.
Likewise, those born in the inverse order and the outcastes are remembered as the impurities among men;
they are to be executed for an offense against a Brahmin, but never shall a fine be imposed upon them.
A man deserving of death shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred suvarṇas;
one deserving of the amputation of a limb shall pay half that amount, and one deserving of a cut on the ear shall pay half of that.
"Beating, binding, and likewise the removal of food—this indeed is the punishment for a Śūdra; there is no monetary fine, says Bṛhaspati. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.9.20)
In this world, one is declared a victor by virtue of fulfilling his promise, through devotion, by honoring the judge and others,
and by the issuance of the document of victory.
A debate is won by one who is inferior through fleeing from an unsurpassed opponent or by resorting to another's side; it is not won by one who has been defeated by his own words.
But if one does not find satisfaction even when [the facts] have been ascertained by the family and others,
the king, having investigated that person's conduct, should again rectify what was wrongly done.
Having reached a decision together with many Brahmins who have mastered the scriptures,
he shall punish the members of the previous court along with the victorious party as being at fault.
And a punishment corresponding to the offense has been prescribed here;
one is declared defeated through witnesses, documents, inference, or properly by means of an ordeal.
He who does not give the prescribed gift shall be banished from that city.
For a Brahmin, no other punishment than branding on the forehead is ordained;
even if he is guilty of a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), a Brahmin does not deserve death. The king should impose exile and the marking [on the forehead], and he should cause him to have his head shaved.
Everything he does—whether gain or loss, decline or rise—is authoritative;
whether in his own country or abroad, no independence shall contradict this.
But he who is appointed by his master to deny the receipt of wealth for the purposes of money-lending, agriculture, or trade, is known as one to whom the funds have been entrusted (nisṛṣṭārtha).
A king must investigate matters of doubt with great care;
in such cases, three parties are benefited while the loss falls upon only one.
The victor obtains wealth and honor; the defeated undergoes discipline and restraint.
Through victory, the king attains merit, as do the members of the assembly through their acts of charity and self-control.
Thus, by carrying out the decisions and protection ordained by the treatises, a king shall spread his fame throughout the world and become equal to Mahendra.
By resolving legal cases through witness testimony, written documents, and inference,
a king spreads his fame in this world and attains the realm of the Sun.
When a king thus understands the definitive conclusion regarding the sacrifice,
he attains glory in this world and goes to the same realm as Śakra.
This legal procedure has been proclaimed together with its constituent parts;
now hear the titles of law which are the causes of dispute.

I shall now explain in due order, according to their true nature, the matters concerning the non-payment of debts, those primarily involving gambling and challenges, and the various types of legal procedures.

That which is to be given and that which is not to be given, by whom, where, and in what manner, as well as the rules for giving and receiving— this is known in the legal tradition as the law of debt (ṛṇādāna).
The interest shall be one-eightieth part [of the principal] month after month when there is security;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per month.
Having received a pledge that is complete, or a bond with a reliable guarantor,
the creditor shall always deliver the debt, whether it be recorded in a document or witnessed by others.
Because it is taken from one who is despised and in distress by those who are free from hesitation,
it is therefore recorded in tradition as being called usury, yielding fourfold or eightfold interest.
In the Purāṇa, the homage... // Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.7 //

Increase is said to be fourfold, proclaimed as fivefold by others, and described as sixfold by yet others; understand them according to their true nature. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.2) [Varieties of Increase] 1.10.8.
The bodily interest, the periodical interest, and another known as the compound interest (cakravṛddhi);
likewise the stipulated interest (kāritā), the crest-interest (śikhāvṛddhi), and the profit on the use of goods (bhogalābha).
Interest may be taken as bodily labor connected with work, or it may be taken monthly;
there is compound interest, interest on interest, wheel-interest, and that which is stipulated by the debtor himself.
That interest which is collected daily is known as "crest-interest" (śikhāvṛddhi);
it grows perpetually like a crest, but ceases upon the cutting off of the head.

But that interest which has been stipulated by the debtor as excessive, being fixed during a time of distress, must always be paid as agreed; otherwise, interest stipulated in any other manner must not be paid under any circumstances. (Br̥haspati 1.10.12)
It grows constantly like a crest, yet it ceases upon the cutting off of the head;
likewise, when the root is provided, this growth of the crest continues—thus it is traditionally taught.
The *stoma* is declared to be the householder's share, and the *śada* is the acquisition of enjoyment from the field.

They say that bodily growth consists of fourfold increase—namely, the increase of wealth, the increase of progeny, and the increase of one's own person; while the fifth is the increase of power (cakravṛddhi).
The creditor may take interest on the principal, as well as physical labor and the acquisition of property, until the principal has been fully repaid. Br̥haspati 1.10.16.
Interest on gold is said to be twofold; on cloth and base metals, threefold;
and on grain, as well as on skins, vehicles, and wool, it is declared to be fourfold. *Bṛhaspati Smṛti* 1.10.17.
The fivefold increase mentioned applies to vegetables; for seeds and grains, it is recorded as sixfold;
for salt, sweat, and meat, the increase is considered eightfold;
and for molasses and honey, when used over a long period, it is likewise stated. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.10.18)
The increase for all types of oils, as well as for liquors, honey, clarified butter,
molasses, and salt, is declared to be eightfold.
The profit on precious stones shall be fivefold; that on cotton shall be fourfold;
and the increase on woods such as sandalwood and the like shall be eightfold.
That interest which is taken in excess of double the principal,
and that which is collected after the full term has expired along with the accrued interest— that usury is censured.
The interest shall increase by one-eightieth part until the principal has doubled;
lent for seven years, it will undoubtedly reach that state in three months less than seven years.
The growth of grass, wood, bricks, thread, leaven, leather, bone, armor, weapons, flowers, and fruits does not cease. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.23)
The interest on gold, grain, and clothing is two, three, and four times the principal respectively;
that on ghee is eightfold, and on copper and similar metals it is fourfold.
The creditor may collect the interest on the principal, as well as the bodily labor and the profit from the enjoyment [of the collateral],
until the principal has been fully repaid.
The others [the intermediate castes] arise from the successive addition of one quarter [of qualities].
In all disputes concerning property, one does not fail through verbal deception;
even if punished for seizing the land or wife of another, one does not lose the property itself.
One should always act with equal increase, but that which is unequal shall cease.
Listen to the rate of interest proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha for a moneylender:
five māṣas on twenty [kārṣāpaṇas]; in this way, the dharma is not violated. (Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.4; Dharmaśāstra 1.10.28)
A māṣa is proclaimed to be one-twentieth of a pala.
In that case, however, if any man shows indifference toward this,
a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him.
Whatever one may obtain for the sake of accomplishing the business of the community, or upon being presented before kings and other authorities, that must be shared equally among all.
Likewise, among those related by lineage and others, this is their eternal law:
that which was acquired through efforts, or preserved, or a debt contracted for the sake of the community.

But he who, even while residing in his own country, does not pay when asked repeatedly, shall pay the interest stipulated by the court, even if he is unwilling. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.5; Bṛhat-Samhitā 1.10.33)
Whether it be for six months or even for a month, the property should be divided according to their respective shares;
or it should be given to those who are destitute, the elderly, the distressed, women, children, the sick, and the diseased.
After three seasons, one may recover the principal along with interest;
in such cases as these, an eightieth part as interest is intended.
That which does not flow out [as interest] would be for the creditor as principal;
even if there is an increase beyond double, in the case of those loans where the interest is periodic,
the king should then decide the matter with those who know the true principles of legal procedure.
But a pledge is used only so long as it is not returned. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.6) (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.37)
A pledge (ādhi) is defined as a bond, and it is said to be of four kinds:
movable and immovable, as well as that which is to be guarded (gopya) and that which is to be enjoyed (bhogya).
Whether it be accidental or with a fixed term, whether recorded in writing or witnessed by others,
when the debt remains unpaid and the stipulated time has expired, the creditor [may act].
If one consumes a pledge out of greed, that profit shall not be realized again;
it must be preserved like a deposit, for interest is lost if it is squandered.

And when there is destruction caused by the king or by fate, just as the pledge would suffer loss, in that case he should cause the pledge to be returned; otherwise, he should pay the debt along with interest.
Whatever is to be given by one held in bondage may be paid through labor or by manual work;
however, when the object is not received, the entire debt shall not be enforced against the debtor against his will.
When the pledge has been used and its value has depreciated, a loss of the principal occurs;
in such a case, the high value is lost, and one should satisfy the debtor.
When a single field is given as a pledge to two parties at the same time,
whoever possesses it first shall obtain its legal title.
When two [items] are presented at the same time, the procedure for giving and selling should be equal; that is what has been proclaimed as the rule.
When the act of depositing, selling,
or giving is performed through a single transaction involving a witness and a document, the document therein serves as proof against any denial.
Kātyāyana declared that a document which is unstipulated, stipulated, qualified in one respect, and further specified in detail is superior.
When the gold has doubled and the stipulated time has expired,
the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge, provided he has waited for two weeks.
If the debtor provides collateral during that interval, he may obtain the pledge;
once the full term has elapsed along with the accrued interest, he shall become the owner of the pledge.
However, if ten days have not yet passed, the debtor is entitled to redeem it.
When a pledge for use has reached twice its value, or when the stipulated time has expired according to the rule,
it should immediately be proclaimed to the debtor's family and then enjoyed [by the creditor].
When gold has doubled in value or when the debtor has disappeared,
the creditor may seize that man's property and sell it in the presence of witnesses.
Or he may keep it for ten days in the presence of a public assembly after its price has been paid;
thereafter, having received a deposit corresponding to the debt, he should relinquish it to another.
If one does not enjoy his own pledge, nor take it back, nor surrender it [to another], then the debtor who has died and whose witness is deceased—the document for him is useless. (Bṛhaspati 1.10.53)
House, water, shops, grain, livestock, women, and vehicles perish through neglect, and likewise fall into a state of worthlessness.
Having secured his own property with men skilled in accounting,
and having it witnessed by his kinsmen and relatives, he would not incur any offense by taking possession of it.
The eighteen-fold dispute, distinguished by its prior and subsequent stages, has been explained; now, understand correctly the various types of legal procedures (kriyā). Bṛhaspati 1.10.56.
An action that was previously performed must be maintained in exactly that same way;
where it is performed otherwise, then there would be a deviation in the ritual act.
Having first abandoned the instrument [of proof], the creditor or the debtor may alter it to be less or more; this is called a "difference in action" (kriyābheda). Br̥had-ārthasaṃhitā 1.10.58.
He who, having undertaken a purpose with two [shares], proceeds with five,
the gain in that case shall be according to the latter, for it is the final one that is certain.
But whatever gift or sale is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings.
By means of each subsequent bond, the preceding bond becomes loosened;
whatever agreement is made later is more powerful than the one before.
When one has made a deposit or a pledge,
and then another person creates a subsequent pledge or a sale, the latter transaction therein is more powerful.
If the sale, the ownership, and the acceptance [of the gift] were all performed on the same day,
and the matter is thus doubtful for all three parties, how should the investigation proceed in that case?
In this matter, they should divide the three means of proof according to their respective shares;
both [the teacher and the student] should receive them in three parts, in accordance with the purpose.
If that debt has been settled through mutual agreement, then the creditor shall not share in the debtor's wealth,
nor shall the debtor be liable for the seizure of property without the consent of both parties.
If a debtor, having paid the principal amount, should demand the release of the pledge, it must be released at that very moment; otherwise, the creditor becomes liable for a fault.
When land or other property has been enjoyed, and subsequently an excess accrues such that the principal and interest have been fully recovered,
the debtor shall recover the pledge.
In the absence of a guarantor, the debtor shall deposit the wealth with the original creditor and obtain the pledge;
when the debtor, having made a formal agreement, gives the field to the money-lender,
then it is certain that the pledge must be released once the debt has been cleared of interest.
"The pledge must be returned by you to me along with interest on the principal;
this is the righteous rule for the practice of lending at interest that has been fully proclaimed."
Where there is an excess of house or field endowed with full enjoyment,
there the debtor shall obtain the pledge and the creditor likewise his debt.
When [the practice] is complete and at its highest degree, that equality of both is proclaimed;
but when it is incomplete, the two should act toward one another according to their respective intentions.

If that [debt] were outstanding, then the creditor would not be entitled to his wealth, nor would the debtor be liable for the pledge, without the mutual consent of both parties. (Bṛhad-ārāṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.72)

In the treatises, the wise have observed four types of surety (*pratibhū*): for appearance, for trust, for payment, and likewise for the delivery of a debt or property. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.7)
One said, "I shall show it"; another spoke, "I am the giver of this wealth"; yet another said, "I shall obtain it. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.74)
But a surety for appearance who produces the person at the proper place and time, or brings forward the security deposit,
shall not be liable therefor, except in the case of an act committed by fate or the king.
The creditor shall allow time for the search of what is lost to the surety,
according to the place, the nature of the object, and its value— whether it be a fortnight, a month, or even half a month.
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance,
he shall pay that debt from his own property to the creditor if he fails to produce him.
The first two [witnesses] shall be made to pay the wealth that was reported at the time of the transaction if it turns out to be false;
as for the latter two, they are liable in case of contradiction, as are their sons in their absence.
A master, one obstructed by enemies, an official, one punished, those under suspicion, an heir alone, a friend, an outcaste, a resident pupil, one following the conduct of a king,
one free from passion, an ascetic, a pauper, a child, an elderly person, a woman, and a sick person are not eligible to be sureties. (Br̥haspati Smṛti 1.10.79)
In the event of the failure of the person placed under obligation, the guarantor must be made to pay for that person.
Indeed, the entire paternal debt must be paid even by the son together with [the father].
But he who, being pressed by the debtor, gives a surety, and is himself subsequently pressed for the debt,
deserves to receive back double that amount after three fortnights have passed.
If, out of a sense of propriety, those of dull intellect and unrefined minds should pay a debt even though they were not made liable for it,
they shall by no means recover from that person the amount for which they were made to pay.
They should not be excessively oppressed; the debt should be made to be paid little by little.
They should not be compelled to act as witnesses against themselves; this is the rule regarding sureties.
If the debtor has disappeared or died, the creditor shall present the document and cause a new deed of location (sthānalekhya) to be executed, specifying the time limit for its validity.
But when money has been paid by a surety to a debtor without being requested,
that amount shall not be made double and returned to the surety by the debtor.
A debtor who has admitted the debt should be made to pay by means of conciliation and other such methods,
as well as through lawful pressure, threats, force, and the confinement of his residence. (Bṛhaspati 1.10.87)

By means of messages from friends and relatives, and by following the method of conciliation, the debtor should generally be made to pay the creditor; this is declared to be the rule of righteousness.
But a Brahmin who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his means.

When a creditor, having brought back wealth requested under false pretenses from a debtor, or having recovered items such as those deposited for safekeeping, causes the debtor to pay, that case is one involving fraud (sopadhi).
When a debtor is made to pay by being brought to his own home and subjected to methods such as beating, that is declared to be "coercion" (balāt-kāra).
A debtor who belongs to the same caste as, or a lower caste than, his creditor may settle the debt with him through manual labor;
however, one of a higher caste must repay it gradually.
One may compel a person of low birth who has become destitute to perform labor for the sake of repaying a debt;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is destitute should be made to pay gradually, according to his income.
Having bound his wife, sons, and cattle, and having made them sit at the door,
where a debtor is made to pay his own debt— that is called *ācarita* (customary practice).
This law applies to one who has admitted [the debt]; however, if he denies it in court, he is made to pay after the matter has been established by means of a document or witnesses.
"I shall give that which is rightfully to be given"—when a debtor speaks thus, he is called a *kriyāvādī* (one who asserts the validity of the legal action). *Bṛhaspati Smṛti* 1.10.96.
One should never obstruct a proponent of action (kriyāvādin) regarding a doubtful matter;
however, one who restrains that which should not be restrained is liable to punishment according to the law.

That matter is declared to be "doubtful" in which both parties may have an error regarding the color, number, and so forth of the object, or even regarding what is to be given and what is not to be given. Br̥hadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārttika 1.10.98.
When the stipulated period has expired and the debt remains unpaid, the creditor may demand repayment from the debtor;
or the debtor may retain the document under an agreement regarding compound interest.
When compound interest (cakravṛddhi) exceeding double [the principal] is stipulated,
then the profit from enjoyment (bhogalābha) shall constitute the principal for men along with its interest.
But he who proceeds with respect to a doubtful matter without having informed the king should be forcibly punished, and that legal matter shall not be established.
Now it is stated what kind of debt, taken from another's hand according to the rules of usury,
must be repaid by whom, where, and how, and when it need not be repaid.
A debt contracted for a short period must be paid when requested;
once the term has expired, it must be repaid with the agreed interest, and in the absence of the father, it must be paid by the sons.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still burdened by debts,
then both his asceticism and his fire-sacrifices shall all belong to the owner of the wealth.
Having brought an indigent debtor to his house, he should make him perform labor;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is a liquor-seller or of similar profession should be made to pay [the debt] very gradually.
Among those who take away wealth, a wife, or a son, the degree of debt increases in the order mentioned last.
In their absence, it goes successively to the other heirs of the estate.
Debts that must be paid:
A debt incurred for religious purposes and the like, which one does not record in writing and does not pay upon demand, shall accrue interest for the creditor. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.10.108)
In such cases, one should cause even the sons to pay the debt of those who are diseased, insane, aged, or long away on travel, even while they are still living.
Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons once it has been proven;
however, this does not apply to those who are born blind, outcastes, the insane, or those afflicted with consumption, leprosy, and similar diseases.
Among those who have entered under a single roof, he who is seen there shall be made to pay;
however, the son of one who has gone abroad shall receive the entire paternal share upon his father's death.
When the father has sent [the son] away, the son shall provide everything from his own share;
however, when the father has died, he shall pay the father's portion, but never the debts of others.
The debt of the father must first be paid, and then one's own;
of those two, the grandfather’s debt must be paid first—thus always should the debt be settled.
A debt contracted by one's father must be paid by the sons once it has been proven;
a debt of a grandfather must be paid equally [by the grandsons], but that of a great-grandfather is not to be paid by his son.
Even one who is dependent for the sake of his family may conduct legal business, whether in his own country or abroad; a learned man should not obstruct him.
Therefore, once a son is born, he must diligently strive to liberate his father from debt so that he does not go to hell by abandoning his own self-interest.
When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares,
whether they are divided or undivided, or whoever may have undertaken that burden.

One should not compel a son to pay for a gift given for the sake of a deity or for a false purpose, nor for what was promised out of lust or anger, nor for a surety-bond, nor for the remainder of a fine or a tax. (Bṛhaspati 1.10.118)
The supervisor of the wives of liquor-sellers, hunters, washermen, cowherds, barbers,
and boatmen shall be made to pay their debts incurred in the business of their husbands.
If a son who incurs debt or misappropriates property is also troublesome,
he shall likewise be the one to take the wife in the absence of an heir to the wealth.
What has been borrowed for the sake of the family by an uncle, a brother’s son, a wife, a slave, a pupil, or a dependent, that the householder ought to pay. (Br̥hadaranyaka 1.10.121)
But he who is appointed by his master to protect wealth and expenditures,
and to engage in lending at interest, agriculture, and trade, is known as one to whom the matter has been entrusted (nisṛṣṭārtha).
He who takes goods such as a camel and the like and does not give them to the owner is born in that owner's house as a slave, a son, a wife, or a beast.
A debt incurred by a son must be cleared by the father if it was approved by him; or he may pay it out of affection for his son, but otherwise he is not obliged to pay it. Bṛhaspati 1.10.124.
...the debtor shall incur bondage; however, having paid the principal at the full term, he may recover the property along with its enjoyment of fruits. Bṛhaspati 1.10.125.

If that [debt] were outstanding, then the creditor would not be entitled to his wealth, nor would the debtor be liable for a pledge, without the mutual consent of both parties. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.126)
When a debtor is summoned by a creditor for the purpose of recovering the debt,
the king shall cause the debtor to pay the amount of the debt as proven by him.
But if one denies the debt while it has been proven by means of evidence,
the judge shall compel him to pay the creditor's claim and a fine according to his capacity.
Whatever amount one may conceal as an object, or whatever amount one may falsely claim in a lawsuit,
both of those ignorant of the Dharma shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.
If one who has received money through a lawful transaction or other means does not record it in writing,
nor deliver it upon demand, that debt shall accrue interest for him.
The law concerning the non-payment of debts, beginning with lending and ending with the methods of compelling payment, has been proclaimed.
Now, let the proper procedure for deposits be heard. (Br̥hadartha 1.11.1)
That which is given unannounced, kept apart, uncounted, unshown,
and marked with a seal, is known as a sealed deposit (upanidhi).
[The Nature of Deposit (Nyāsa):
When property is placed in another's house out of fear of kings, thieves, or enemies, or due to deception by heirs, that is proclaimed to be a deposit (nyāsa). Bṛhad-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.11.2–3.

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.11.3: The Method of Establishing] Having examined the location—the house and the site—as well as that debt, the various qualities, truthfulness, purity, and kinsmen, one should establish the treasure. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.11.4.
Furthermore, that [debt] is said to be of two kinds: one with a witness and the other otherwise.
Likewise, in the case of its reversal, there should be a counter-transaction or a formal acknowledgment.
That [debt] is declared to be of two kinds: that given openly and that given in secret;
it must be protected like a son, for it perishes through neglect.
Whatever merit may come from giving gold, base metals, garments, and so forth, that same merit shall belong to one who protects a deposit,
as well as one who has sought refuge.
Just as there would be fault for a woman in betraying her husband, or for a man in killing his son or friend,
so too is there fault for men in consuming or neglecting a deposit.
One should not accept property placed in trust; its loss brings dishonor.
What has been accepted should be protected with effort, and what was requested once should be returned.

Whatever has been established by which procedure, and whatever has been manifested by whom, that very thing must be given to him; what is not to be given is that which is immediately contrary [to the rule].
If, due to an injury caused by the king of the gods (Indra), that [deposit] should be destroyed,
there is no fault in that case, provided it is accompanied by the property of the depositor.
If the borrower, having received a deposit with a specific distinction and with indifference, should destroy it,
or should not return it when asked for, he shall be compelled to pay it back along with interest.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.11.7: His punishment for enjoyment:

Whoever accomplishes his own business by means of property entrusted to him shall be punished by the king and shall be made to pay that [property] along with interest. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.11.13)
If a person, having received a deposit, denies it— whether by means of witnesses or by oath— the judge,
having established the truth, shall compel him to restore the deposit and impose a fine equal to its value.
Where a dispute arises concerning a secret deposit,
it is traditionally taught that an ordeal is the means of investigation for both parties.
If a gift was made privately by someone, or accepted privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking back.
One would obtain nothing from the ocean if one were not to draw from it.
This same rule is declared to apply to property that has been deposited, borrowed, given by an artisan, placed as a pledge, or held under a lien, as well as to one who has come for refuge.
But if a deposit is being processed and remains unfinished after a fixed number of days have passed,
the artisan, even if struck by misfortune, shall be made to pay for it upon its subsequent delivery.
One who gives what has been requested and authorized by the owner does not commit an offense.
Immediately after the section on deposits, the sale by one who is not the owner was proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Listen to that with diligence; I shall explain it to you in detail. (Bṛh. 1.12.1)
One who deals with deposits, goods sent for delivery, trusts, what has been taken, what has been borrowed,
pledges, secret sales, or public sales, is declared to be a non-owner. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.12.1–2)
But for one who has purchased [an item] at a price after it was previously reported to the official,
no fault exists; he would not be a thief, because the purchase was made through deception.

[The definition of selling at a loss (upavikraya): That which is purchased within the house, outside the village, at night, from an unreliable person, or for a low price— this is to be known as selling at a loss.

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.12.4–5: Determination of the Purity of the Purchaser] But if the former owner comes and investigates that property, the price must be shown; from that, the purity of the purchaser shall be established. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.12.5: In that case, the price must be demonstrated; from that, the purchaser's innocence shall follow.
Once the original price has been recovered, the purchaser can by no means be prosecuted;
for the dispute regarding the price does not cease for one who has lost the property.
Where the seller is produced [as a witness] and thus loses the legal case,
he shall pay the purchase price and a fine to the king, and the value of the property to the owner.
He who, being a non-owner, covets another's property out of greed,
and subsequently fails to relinquish it, shall be compelled to pay a fine double the value of that property.

But in a debate lacking authoritative means of proof, O King, the monarch himself should make the final decision based on the relative status of the persons involved, whether they be equal, inferior, or superior.
Where a stolen object is found within a marketplace and recognized by the king's officers, yet was purchased from an unknown source, or where the seller has died; ||| Brh_1,12.10 |||
The owner, having paid half the value, may recover his own property;
in that case, according to legal procedure, half of the value of both [the stolen object and the price paid] shall be forfeited.
Failure to recognize the price and likewise failure to protect it—
these two have been declared by the Buddhas to be causes of the loss of wealth.
If it is discovered by royal officers that [the object] was obtained from a market street and seized during the day,
the wealthy purchaser obtains the wealth.
If one who has sold land does not establish the purchaser's possession, he must restore that property to him;
otherwise, he shall be liable to the punishment for theft.

These two have been declared by the Buddhas to be causes for the loss of wealth: that which is not recognized as having specific qualities, and that for which no price can be obtained. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.12.15)
In that case, an equal loss should be assigned to both the purchaser and the non-believer.

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13: Joint Undertaking] [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.1: Those Eligible for Joint Action] (p.129) By those who are of noble birth, skillful, untiring, wise, and knowledgeable in monetary matters;
One should carry out affairs together with those who are pure, brave, and knowledgeable regarding income and expenditure.
Whatever portion of anything is equal, excessive, or deficient,
its depletion, expenditure, and increase will likewise be of that same nature.
Those who lack qualification:

"The wise should not perform activities such as trade and the like together with those who are incapable, lazy, afflicted by disease, unfortunate, or without support. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.2–3)
But for those who carry out a transaction with gold, grain, liquids, and so forth,
their profit shall be of a corresponding kind, according to equal, deficient, or superior shares.

If a share that is equal, deficient, or excessive has been cast [into the dice], he by whom it was cast shall likewise pay the loss, perform the work, and receive the profit. || Br̥had-Āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.5 ||

[Br̥h. 1.13.4–6: The Conclusion of Those Discussions] Those very same individuals are declared to be both the examiners and the witnesses for one another regarding a disputed matter, provided they are not motivated by deceit, nor possessed by hatred or affection.
Whosoever among them is known to be a cheat in buying or selling shall be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies to every kind of dispute.

[Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.5: Determination regarding loss of goods] When a loss occurs there due to acts of gods or kings, it is declared to belong to all [the partners]; it should be apportioned accordingly according to their shares. Br̥h 1.13.8.
But if one who has not been specifically designated should, through negligence, cause the property to be lost while it is being withheld,
he alone must provide that which is to be given to all the partners.
Having given a sixth part to the king, they shall receive their shares as prescribed.
[The tenth part for the protector: Out of fear of gods and kings, let him protect [the people] according to his own ability;
having given him a tenth part, they may take another portion from that share. Brh_1,13.11.
When a merchant arrives at a customs station, he should pay the toll as is appropriate;
he should not deviate from that, for this is proclaimed to be the tribute due to kings. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.7, 12)
It is not so when a calamity from thieves, kings, or fire has arisen;
however, for one who protects [the goods] according to his own ability, a tenth part is prescribed as his share.

[Br̥h. 1.13.8–14: Decision regarding the loss of one among those performing joint labor] When, in that case, some merchant should die through negligence, his goods must be displayed by the appointed royal officers. Br̥h. 1.13.14.
When someone arrives, that man who is the heir to the inheritance must demonstrate his ownership before others; only then does he deserve to receive it.
The king should take a sixth part, or likewise a ninth or a tenth;
from those of the Śūdra and Vaiśya castes, he should take a twentieth part from the Brāhmaṇa.
But if the owner does not come forward by any means after three years, then the king shall take that property; however, he should bestow the property of a Brahmin upon other Brahmins.
Thus, when anyone among those engaged in the performance of rites passes away,
the funeral rites must be performed by his kinsman together with all the assistants.
The Adhvaryu priest shall take the chariot, and the Brahman priest the horse at the fire-consecration;
the Hotṛ priest the horse that chooses the *nivid* verses, and the Udgātṛ priest the cart at the purchase [of the Soma].
Among all [the priests], the principal ones are entitled to half; others entitled to a half are entitled to half of that;
those entitled to a third receive a third part, and those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth part.

They are declared to be of three kinds: those who are newcomers, those who have come down by succession, and likewise those who are self-made; one should conduct oneself toward them in that very same way.
[The manner of joint action:
If a man, being approved by many, should himself give wealth or cause it to be given, it shall be considered as performed by all of them. Br̥h. 1.13.22.
A debt to kinsmen, relatives, and friends may be paid even with collateral;
for others, it must be accompanied by a guarantor, as well as a written document and witnesses.
Gold may be given at one's own will, but liquids and grain must be given with a time-limit;
they should be given according to local custom, and likewise they should be received.
But that which is given by those assembled together must likewise be requested;
and whoever does not ask for it is deprived of his gain.
[Regarding the collective performance of agricultural work: Listen; this procedure for farmers and others is now being declared. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.26)
A wise man should engage in agriculture together with those who are equal to him in terms of draft animals, drivers, seeds, and other implements for the field.
Where a loss of the field occurs due to the failure of external seeds,
that loss must be made good by that very person for all those who live by agriculture.
One should carefully avoid a field that is saline, infested with mice, located on a mountain, near a city, or by a royal highway. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya 1.13.29)
One who sows at the proper time in a field that is provided with ditches, situated near water, well-irrigated, and endowed with fertile soil on all sides, reaps an excellent harvest.
A wise farmer should not hire one who is emaciated, excessively old, low-born, diseased, a fugitive, one-eyed, or lame; rather, he should employ an outsider.
This ancient law of the plowmen has been fully declared.

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.12 śilpinaḥ] "The wise have declared that a craftsman is one who is skilled in the arts and is the one who refines gold, base metals, thread, wood, stone, and leather. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.33.
Where goldsmiths and others perform their craft collectively,
they shall receive wages according to their work, in proportion to their respective shares.
Teachers who are skilled in the sciences and those who are masters of the arts shall receive one,
two, three, or four shares, respectively, in ascending order.
For those who, having come together, construct a mansion, a temple, or even the furnishings for a righteous purpose,
the leader among them deserves two shares.
This indeed is the rule for dancers proclaimed by the virtuous:
one who knows the rhythm receives one and a half shares, while the singers receive equal shares.
[The Division of the Gain of Thieves:

But that which has been recovered from a foreign land by thieves at the command of their master, they shall divide among themselves according to their respective shares after giving one-sixth to the king. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.38)
Then, the chief hero shall receive four shares;
the capable one shall take two shares; and all the rest shall receive equal shares.

Thus has been declared in its entirety the expiation for collective offenses arising from association. Now, the rules regarding what should not be given, what may be given, what has been given, and what has not been given shall be explained.
Common property, sons, wives, and so forth, one's entire estate, a deposit, that which has been requested,
and likewise what has been promised to another— these eight kinds of things are traditionally held to be not to be given away.
That which remains after providing for one's family and [their] food and clothing should be given;
otherwise, the gift of the donor would have the taste of honey followed by poison, and his religious merit (dharma) would be lost.
Whatever field is acquired from a garden or a house-site,
whether inherited from a father or obtained by oneself— that which is intended for distribution must be given away.

That which is given at one's own will, that which is acquired by oneself, a pledge according to the custom of pledging, and property obtained through marriage or inherited in succession— in these cases, no gift whatsoever is prohibited.
That which is obtained as a dowry, inherited in succession, or acquired through valor,
as well as that which is given with the permission of the wife, kinsmen, or the owner, shall attain validity.
Except for his entire estate and his home, whatever property he possesses for the maintenance of his family and other such needs is his own to give; otherwise, it shall not be given.
Whether they are divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights to immovable property;
for a single heir has no power over any of it regarding its gift, mortgage, or sale.
Wages, that which is given out of satisfaction, the price for goods, the bride-price,
a gift to one who has rendered assistance, and that given through faith, favor, or affection— this is remembered as the eightfold gift.
A gift given to a Śūdra is said to be equal [in merit]; to a Vaiśya, it is remembered as being twice that;
a gift to a Kṣatriya is threefold, and to a Brāhmaṇa, it is remembered as being sixfold.
For a Śrotriya, it is one thousand; for a teacher (upādhyāya), twice that;
for an Ācārya, it should be known as threefold; and for those who have maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), it is twice that.
One thousandfold for one who knows the Ātmika; infinite for an Agnihotrin;
one hundred thousandfold for a Soma-sacrificer; and infinite for a knower of Brahman.
A woman should bestow her property upon her own kinsmen, avoiding [unworthy] persons;
in the absence of kinsmen, however, it goes to her relatives; and in their absence, to the twice-born.
That which is given after my death shall not bring merit to living beings;
because it has not been given by me while alive, it shall fall to the heir upon my passing.
By those who are angry, joyful, intoxicated, afflicted, childish, insane, or overcome by fear; by the drunk, the very old, the dissolute, the deluded, and those overwhelmed by the force of grief.
Likewise, that which was given by Nandadatta is proclaimed by them as "that which was not given."
If a gift is given with the desire for personal gain, to an unworthy recipient while suspecting them to be worthy,
or for a purpose connected with unrighteousness, the owner shall recover it.
One who consumes what has not been given should be punished, as should one who gives what ought not to be given.
The rules regarding what is not to be given and so forth have been declared; now the rule for those who are maintained is being stated.
Having undertaken service, this first point is proclaimed at the outset. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.15.1)
But when one, having undertaken service, does not perform it, this legal ground of dispute is called "non-fulfillment of service after undertaking it. (Bṛhaspati 1.15.2)
The non-payment of wages and the dispute between the owner and the keeper for that purpose are prescribed in due order; however, this constitutes the threefold classification of hired laborers.
However, she has been described in many ways according to her birth and actions;
she is fourfold by reason of knowledge, realization, desire, and wealth.
Furthermore, each one of these is further divided according to the distinction of its functions.
The triple Vidyā is declared to be characterized by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
for its sake, one should perform the service of the teacher as enjoined.
Craftsmanship is said to be the working of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as dancing and the like; having acquired that, he should perform service in the house of his guru.
He who enjoys the wife of another should be known as one hired by a mare;
he should perform work for her husband, just as a man is supported by food.
One is said to be a bearer of many meanings, while another is a bearer of parts;
furthermore, the states of being inferior, middling, or superior have been declared for all of them indeed.
Likewise, one who maintains [the practice] for a day, half a month, six months, three months,
or a year shall perform the prescribed action and obtain what has been declared.
A hired servant is to be known as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior;
their wages, based on the work performed, should correspond to their capacity and devotion.
Among these, the warrior is the highest, the cultivator is the middling, and the porter is the lowest; such is the threefold classification of the hired laborer.
The warrior is declared the highest, the farmer the middling,
and the burden-bearer as well as the householder is declared the lowest.
The livelihood of those who subsist on agriculture and cattle is traditionally held to be of two kinds;
from the grain produced and likewise from milk, he shall obtain [his sustenance], of this there is no doubt.
For these four are declared to be performers of auspicious work:
the student, the apprentice, the hired servant, and the laborer.
But the remaining fifteen types of slaves partake only of the lowest forms of work.
Action is also said to be of two kinds: indeed, the inauspicious and the auspicious.
The inauspicious is called the work of a slave, while the auspicious is remembered as the work of a laborer.

The cleaning of the house door, impure places, the street, and the refuse heap; the touching of the limbs of one's own household, and the taking up and discarding of food remnants, feces, and urine. // Brh_1,15.17 //
Furthermore, attending upon one's master while he is traveling by means of one's own limbs should be understood as impure action; other than this, it is pure.
From that time forward, he should be called one protected by the favor of his master;
his food may be eaten and gifts accepted from him, and he becomes esteemed by the virtuous.
Until he has grasped [the truth], the student, being self-restrained, should serve his teacher;
his conduct toward the teacher’s wife and likewise toward the teacher’s son should be the same.
And having returned, after presenting the teacher’s fee to the guru, he returns home; this is declared to be the conduct of a student.
In this matter, the first four classes are not released from servitude except through the favor of their master; for them, servitude is hereditary.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—
of all these he is the most wretched, for even he is not released from servitude.

If a woman is married by a slave, she becomes his slave; he too shall attain the status of a slave, because the husband is her master, and since the master's authority is dependent upon his own owner.
And those sons born of a female slave by her husband or by another man—
if the progenitor is the master, the lord shall not compel the female slave to work as a slave.
The plowman who provides his own oxen shall take a third or a fifth part of the crop;
one who is supported by food and clothing shall take a fifth part from the plowing.
Furthermore, from a field where the crop has grown, he may take one-third, provided he has not been supported by them.
A hired servant must not commit even the slightest act of deception against his master;
he incurs a loss of wages, and from that, a legal dispute arises.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.1: Determination regarding the non-performance of work by one who has been hired.
If one who has been hired, being not ill, should out of pride fail to perform the work as directed, he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid. (Br̥h. 1.16.4)
[The Punishment for One Who Has Received Wages] When a hired laborer who has received wages does not perform the work,
if he is capable, he shall be made to pay a fine and twice that amount as wages. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.16.5)
One who abandons work after having received wages shall pay double;
for one who has not received wages, the penalty is equal to the amount due. If wages have not been paid, the employer must provide maintenance and protect the tools.
[The Punishment for Failing to Fulfill a Promise] He who, having made a promise, does not fulfill it, should be compelled to do so even by force;
if he still does not perform that action, he shall incur a fine of twenty [paṇas]. (Bṛhad-ārāṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.4–7)
He shall be fined eight kṛṣṇalas, and his wages shall not be paid.
Whatever improper action a servant performs while being directed by his master, the master incurs the fault for that purpose. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.5–9)
[The occasions when the herdsman is free from fault:
"In the case of an act of fate, or by the king's decree, or likewise during the upheaval of the kingdom;
whatever may be lost or stolen, the herdsman is not culpable therein. (Bṛhad-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.6, 10)

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.7: The Master’s Rule on Punishment] When the work has been performed, if the master does not pay the wages to the laborer, he shall be compelled by the king to pay them, and a fine shall be imposed in proportion to the offense. Br̥h. 1.16.11.
[The Punishment for the Fault of the Herdsman] But if there is destruction due to the fault of the herdsman, a fine is prescribed for the herdsman:
twelve and a half paṇas, and the value of the property itself must be paid to the owner. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.16.8, 12)
If she is ill, exhausted, distracted, or occupied with royal duties,
and yet does not come when invited, she is considered an irreproachable *baḍabā*.
Likewise, one who has been hired for milk shall receive all of it on the eighth day;
he shall deliver it all in the evening... // Brh_1,16.14 //
Without exerting himself, without raising a cry, and without informing his master,
the cowherd must bear that [loss] and pay a fine to the king.
One should protect [the property] from the fear of worms, thieves, and tigers, as well as from caves and pits;
one should recover it by all possible means, or, if it is within the range of a *krośa*, report it to the owner.
One should drive the cows away from the crops; for if they have fed upon them, two faults arise:

the owner shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], and the herdsman deserves corporal punishment. Furthermore, if the crop has been consumed with its roots, the fine is both the value of the damage and a hundred [paṇas].
This indeed has been fully described as the conduct between masters and servants. Now, learn in brief the rules for making a formal agreement. Bṛh. 1.17.1.
Having summoned Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, well-versed in the scriptures, and maintainers of the sacred fire-offering,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
The king should grant them house-sites with the right to unimpeded taxation,
and having recorded this in his own edicts, he should ensure they remain free from all burdens.
They shall perform the daily rites, the occasional rites, those for specific desires, as well as those for pacification and nourishment;
likewise, they shall provide a definitive decision regarding matters of doubt.
[The performance of religious duties by association: But for the sake of the village, the guild, or the corporation, a convention and the performance of agreements should be made;
that [convention] must be carried out in times of distress, and likewise in matters of religious duty. (Br̥h. 1.17.5)
