Fear of deceitful thieves and affliction are known to be common to all;
therefore, their pacification must be undertaken by everyone collectively, not by any single individual alone.
Having first established mutual trust through a deposit, a written contract, or neutral mediators, they should thereafter carry out their business affairs. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.17.3, 1.17.7)

Those who are hostile, addicted to vices, modest, lazy, or timid; those who are unfit for employment; the greedy, the very old, and children—these should not be appointed as counselors in matters of statecraft.
Those who are pure, knowers of the Vedic dharma, skillful, self-controlled, of noble birth,
and proficient in all tasks— these most excellent men should be appointed [as officiants].
Two, three, or five persons should be appointed who speak for the welfare of the community;
their word must be carried out by the village, guilds, assemblies, and so forth.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.17.5: A Compact Agreement] The construction of assembly halls, water-stations, temples, ponds, and gardens;
likewise, the improvement of the conditions for the helpless and the poor, and the performance of works of public utility.
We must each perform our share of providing shelter and ensuring their cessation;
that this document has been written in this manner constitutes a righteous formal agreement.
Those who are capable must protect [the weak]; however, for one who is capable but violates [this duty], the punishment shall be the confiscation of all his property and banishment from the city.
In that regard, whatever man creates a division or shows indifference [toward the teacher],
a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him.
But he who would injure common property, or revile one learned in the three Vedas, or obstruct a formal agreement or a ritual act, should be banished from that city.
One who inflicts wounds, a slanderer, a creator of dissension, as well as one who commits violence,
and one who hates a guild, a corporation, or the king, shall be swiftly banished from there.
The heads of families, guilds, and corporations, as well as those residing in cities and fortresses,
shall impose verbal censure, fines, or banishment upon evildoers.

The punishment and favor toward men that have been carried out by them according to their own duty must also be approved by the king, for they are traditionally considered to have been delegated with full authority.
For those who have become possessed by hatred may cause harm to even a single person.
When a conflict arises between the assemblies and their leaders,
the king should investigate the matter and establish them upon their proper path.
... whoever is capable of violating [this rule], his punishment shall be the confiscation of all property and banishment from the city. Bṛh. 1.17.21.
Those who, having come together and made one person their representative, seize what is due to the king,
as well as merchants who flee, shall be made to pay eightfold.
Whatever one may obtain from that, it shall be shared equally among all;
whether it be for six months or for a month, it must be divided according to their respective shares.
Or rather, it should be given to the poor, the elderly, the blind, women, children, and the sick;
likewise to those seeking offspring and others—for this is the eternal law.
Whether acquired through great efforts, protected with care, staked for the sake of the community,
or obtained through the favor of the king— it is equal for all members.
This determination of conventional practice has been stated in brief;
now hear this dispute arising from buying and selling. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.18.1)
Two kinds of property are declared: the movable and the immovable.
At the time of purchase, the term "merchandise" (paṇya) is traditionally applied to both.
[The Punishment for Selling Defective Goods] If an unwise man, knowing that a commodity is defective, sells it,
he shall be made to pay double that very amount, as well as an equal fine as a penalty. *Bṛhaspati Smṛti* 1.18.2–3.

[Br̥h. 1.18.3–4: Things to be relinquished] What has been sold by one who is intoxicated or insane, for a low price, or out of fear; or what has been relinquished by one who is not independent or is deluded—this must be returned to him. Br̥h. 1.18.4.
But he who, having sold it into the hand of one person, delivers it to another,
shall be made to pay double that amount as a fine, and the same amount as a disciplinary penalty.

The periods for examination are ten days, one day, five days, seven days, a month, three days, and half a month; these apply respectively to seeds, iron, draft animals, jewels, women, milch cattle, and men. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.18.4–6)
If, however, any defect or blemish should arise in the article prior to that time,
it must be returned to the seller, and the buyer shall recover the purchase price.

But if something is purchased without being examined and is later discovered to be defective, that purchased commodity must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned.
One should personally examine a commodity and show it to others;
having accepted what has been examined and approved by many, one should not reject it again.
The examination of horses, silver, gold, grain, iron, goats, garments, and products made of leather or wood shall last for one day.
The valuation of horses, mules, and female donkeys is determined by their physical characteristics;
for goods kept in marketplaces, it is by the king's command; and for cattle and land, it is by the mutual agreement of both parties.
In the sharing and exchange of both fields,
the accomplishment of their purpose will come about through the mindfulness performed by those two.
If those standing nearby—such as the purchaser, kinsmen, and so forth—are remembered, they should be questioned;
otherwise, if the ritual act has been performed, one should then show the consent of the kinsmen.
The purchase of immovable property is held to be valid only through the testimony of relatives and others;
otherwise, if it should be a purchase made in another village, [the validity] depends on three fortnights.
Full brothers, sapindas, sodakas, and those of the same lineage (gotra),
as well as neighbors and creditors— these seven are considered the sources from whom [the heirs] are to be taken.
If a higher or lower price is paid than what is appropriate for the value, it is considered improper;
however, once the purchase is finalized, it cannot be annulled even after hundreds of years.
Bṛhaspati states that in all sales, one should have recorded the wells, trees, and so forth,
as well as waterways and whatever else exists, by other means as well.

They say that a field endowed with [auspicious] qualities, a tree with ripened grain, or fruit fit for enjoyment; likewise a well, a pond, a house, and a high mound—these belong to the seller when they are being sold to a buyer. *Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-smṛti* 1.18.18.
An exchange has been made with those who are intoxicated, deluded, ignorant, distressed, or confused;
whatever in that transaction was of an improper value, all of that shall be rescinded. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.18.19)
Relatives, neighbors, and creditors who have gone outside the village for a purchase do not deserve to object, once the property has been acquired in due order over the course of three fortnights.
Or else, one may attain that [result] after three fortnights or after three months.
This rule has been set forth regarding disputes over purchase and sale; now learn the law concerning boundary disputes over villages, fields, houses, and so forth. Br̥h. 1.19.1.
And they should establish boundary trees— *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, *kiṃśuka*,
*śālmalī*, *śāla*, and *tāla*.
And likewise milky trees. // Brh_1,19.2 //
Bushes, various types of bamboos, śamī trees, creepers, and plots of land, as well as reeds,
kubjaka shrubs, and thickets— in this manner, the boundary is not lost.
Ponds, wells, and springs,
as well as temples of the deities, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries.
Having granted the land, the king shall demarcate it as being overseen by the four classes of physicians, merchants, village officials, all the villagers, the local headman, and the proprietor's men.
If a Śūdra should be the leader, one should adorn him with the ornament of impotence, smear his face with the ashes of a corpse,
make five finger-marks on his chest with the blood of a sacrificial animal, fasten intestines around his neck, and he should hold a clod of earth from a boundary with his right hand upon his head.
At the time of settling [the village], the determination of the boundary must be made;
it should be marked with both public and secret signs to remove all doubt.
By their very nature, things that are imperishable do not conflict with one another;
such as ponds, wells, tanks, shrines, groves, and temples. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.19.8)
High ground, low ground, the course of rivers, reeds, thickets, mountains, and so forth—
these should always be made as visible marks for the boundary.
If there should be doubt even when signs are observed,
the determination of the boundary in a dispute must depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.19.10)
And in the absence of witnesses, four inhabitants living on the borders of the village shall, being purified,
determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
But in the absence of neighboring villagers who are witnesses to the boundary,
one should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests.
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest.
Whatever marks they may describe when questioned regarding the boundaries between two villages, the king shall establish those exactly so in accordance with the law.
Placing their heads upon the earth, wearing garlands and red garments,
and being sworn by their respective meritorious deeds, they shall speak the truth.
One should thus fix the boundary and record all those [markers] by name;
one should always cause these visible signs to be made at the boundary.
Likewise, he should establish other hidden signs which the earth would not consume;
he should also cause other boundary markers to be made that serve as protective covers.
Seeing that the world is constantly subject to reversal, one should understand the boundary of existence:
there are bones in the cremation ground, as well as cow-hair, ashes, and skull-fragments. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.19.18)
He should cause cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel,
and sand to be placed at the junctions of the boundary so that they remain hidden from view.
Cow-dung, bones, husks, charcoal, gravel, stones,
potsherds, sand, bricks, cow-hair, cotton-seeds, bones, and ashes.
Having placed these items in jars, one should have them deposited at the boundaries of the boundary-markers;
then, one should carefully show them to children of tender age.
And likewise, they should show those children [the boundary] when they have reached old age;
in this way, through knowledge passed down in succession, no confusion regarding the boundary arises.
By the power of fortune or misfortune, it effects the taking away or the giving of gifts for men;
just as on one side there is the collapse of the earth's slope, while on the other there is its stability.
One should not displace the boundary-mark that has been established on a riverbank;
when a field with standing crops is overstepped, the ground itself becomes severed.

The owner of the field shall regain that land which was taken away by the king through anger or greed, either by force or by legal means, just as a river regains its course by the flow of its current.
In disputes concerning houses and fields, the decision is reached based on the testimony of neighbors;
as well as those who are the heads of city or village corporations, and those men who are the most venerable.
Agriculturists, artisans, laborers, cowherds, hunters, those who live by gleaning, root-diggers, fishermen, those who breach irrigation channels, and those who cause harm; Brh_1,19.27 //
Those who know the title deed, the means of proof, the possession, the desire, the name,
and the characteristics of the specific plot of land— they are the witnesses in this matter.
But she who was given by him while he was pleased shall not attain success,
[if she was taken away by the king through anger or greed, or by fraud or even by legal means].
If land has been seized from one who enjoys it without legal title,
or if it has been given to one superior in merit, one must never displace that person from it.
Bound by their respective oaths, they shall declare the determination regarding the boundary;
they shall point out hidden deposits, for that is the established rule of evidence.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by means of truth, and a Kṣatriya by means of his vehicle and weapons.
Even a single virtuous person, recognized by both sides as being free from the marks of a knower,
may wear red garlands and garments and take earth upon his head.
A man who is devoted to truth and has observed a fast should point out the boundary.
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary,
the king shall punish them all individually with the middle amercement.
Those witnesses of truth who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
This rule has been proclaimed for every stationary legal proceeding.
And those neighboring witnesses who have arisen from that [group] and reside in another region are designated as "primary" (maula); they should be questioned for the determination of the case.
But whatever those who are free from malice, impartial, and of equal conduct may say regarding a doubtful matter, that must be accepted as authoritative; in this way, dharma is not lost.
When land is acquired from another village and given to someone else, it shall be otherwise; for men, any gain resulting from the king or from fate is subject to different rules.
In the case of a great river, or when land is granted by a king, how can there be any deliberation?
Land released by a river or given by a king belongs to him alone who possesses it; otherwise, the acquisition of land by men would depend solely on chance or fate.
The decline, rise, and very life of men are subject to the power of fate and the king;
therefore, at all times, one should not oppose what has been ordained by them.
Wherever a river has been established as the boundary between two villages,
it effects the giving and taking [of land] according to the fortune or misfortune of men;
and by its fluctuation through increase or decrease, even a small amount, it deserves punishment for causing displacement.
The king shall establish an uneven boundary, determined by markers, for a district of ten villages, a hundred villages, a thousand villages, or a hundred thousand villages.
From the time of its construction, whatever house, shop, or other property was enjoyed by whomsoever, in what measure, and in what manner, that should not be altered for them.
Likewise, one should not disturb the windows, the drainage channels, the turrets, the altars, or the chariot-paths already established in a four-winged house.
One should not obstruct the girdle, the water-channel, the spout, or the window;
by damaging a drain or the site of a house, one shall be liable to a fine.
After the time of settling into a residence, these [rites] should not be performed in any way; [they are] not to be done during the construction of a house.
One should not construct a drainage channel or a water-pipe that falls within the sight of another's dwelling.
One should never, under any circumstances, construct a place for the sacred fire, a pit, or a receptacle for pouring out the remains of water offerings too close to another person's wall.
One should construct embankments for excrement, urine, and water, as well as a fire-place and a drainage pit,
at a distance of two cubits from the wall of another's property.
That by which people and animals go and come without restraint is called *saṃsaraṇa*; it must not be obstructed by anyone.
He who, out of desire, creates a mixture [of castes], fills a pit, plants trees [inappropriately], or voids excrement there, shall be fined one *māṣaka*.
Having taken [the grain], he should transport it at the proper time for the sake of protection and storage;
if he fails to do so, he must pay the owner half of the harvested yield.
If anyone, having taken a field, neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated,
he shall be made to pay the share to the owner and a fine equal to that amount to the king.
If the [oblation] is offered late, it is the tenth; likewise, if drawn out, it is the eighth;
but if well-prepared, it shall be the sixth, having been determined according to the rule.
Harshness of speech consists of unpleasant words and physical striking; it is recorded as being of two kinds.
Each of these is further divided into three types, and punishment is said to possess three characteristics. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.20.1)
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.20.1–2: The threefold nature of verbal abuse] Insulting the laws of a country, one's family, and so forth,
or associating someone with sin without using material wealth— this is called the first type of verbal abuse.
The verbal accusation of a minor offense (upapātaka) involving a sister or a brother is declared by those who know the scriptures to be middling harshness of speech.
The discourse on forbidden foods and drinks, the defilement by mortal sins,
harshness of speech, and the intense act of causing one to fall into a pit— these are declared to be the highest [forms of verbal abuse].
But regarding verbal abuse between those of equal caste and qualities,
the prescribed punishment in the treatise is a fine of twelve and a half panas.
For those who are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly disabled, the fine shall likewise be two kārṣāpaṇas.
For insulting someone of one's own caste, the fine is twelve and a half paṇas;
for insulting someone of a lower caste, the fine is six paṇas and one kākiṇī.

In cases of mutual verbal abuse, the punishment for those who are equal is the same; however, for one who is inferior, it is double, and for one who is superior, it is said to be greater than that— just as in the case of the blind, the lame, and others.
If one insults a sister or other such relative, he shall be fined fifty paṇas;
however, a Brahmin does not incur guilt for verbal abuse directed at one who is deficient in merit.
By calling one who has fallen "fallen," or again, by calling a thief a "thief," one incurs an equal fault through such speech. ... ... // Bṛh 1.20.10 //
If a king unjustly administers instruction on dharma to Brahmins according to his own whim,
the king shall cause boiling oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
If a Kṣatriya accuses a Brahmin, his fine shall be fifty;
likewise for a Vaiśya, it is twenty-five, and for a Śūdra, twelve and a half.
This discipline has been prescribed for a Śūdra who is truthful and innocent;
however, even if he is devoid of merit and speaks harshly, a Brāhmaṇa must not commit an offense against him.
A Vaiśya who reviles a Kṣatriya should be made to pay a fine;
a Kṣatriya who insults a Vaiśya deserves punishment equal to half of that amount.
For reviling a Śūdra, the fine for a Kṣatriya is twenty-five [paṇas];
for a person of high status, it is stated by those learned in the scriptures that the fine there is double.
A Śūdra who slanders a Vaiśya should be made to pay the first fine;
for slandering a Kṣatriya, the middle fine; and for slandering a Brāhmaṇa, the highest amercement.
One who defames another by [attributing] a country or other such things shall be made to pay twelve and a half paṇas;
one who, out of arrogance, joins another with a crime shall be made to pay the first amercement.
One who imparts instruction on the Dharma accompanied by citations from the Vedas, but who insults Brahmins, shall be punished by the cutting off of his tongue. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.20.18)

This punishment has been fully declared by me with respect to men; it should be determined by the wise according to the degree of equality, deficiency, or excess [of the offense]. Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.20.19.
[Assault with violence:
Assault with violence is said to consist of striking with hands, stones, or clubs; with ashes, mud, or dust; or with weapons and missiles. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.21.1)
Whatever punishment is prescribed for one who has committed verbal abuse,
he shall cause that very same punishment to be inflicted twice, except in the case of death.
When two persons strike each other with a staff, the punishment is traditionally held to be equal;
however, the one who initiates the assault and the one who persists in it shall be made to pay a higher fine.
If one who has been previously reviled reviles in return, or strikes back when struck,
or even kills an assassin, that man incurs no guilt.

If a base person should insult a virtuous man through verbal abuse and the like, it is that very person whom the king should strike; he must not seek out the fault of the victim. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.21.5)
[First, Assault] Throwing ashes and the like, as well as striking with the hand or other means,
constitutes the first degree of assault; in this case, a fine of one *māṣa* shall be imposed.
This punishment has been declared for equal [wives] and for the wives of others;
it should be understood by the wise as being double or triple, depending on the relative status [of the woman].
For raising a stone, a slab, or a piece of wood [against another], the first amercement shall be imposed;
likewise, for striking one another with hands or feet, the fine shall be ten and twenty paṇas respectively.
When two parties have become agitated during the preparation for weapons, a middle fine should be applied; however,
when the blow has actually fallen, the wise should impose a punishment proportionate to the act committed at the moment of impact.
If one strikes with bricks, stones, or wood, the fine shall be two māṣas;
if blood is drawn, the wise should impose double the punishment.
For piercing the skin, the first amercement is the punishment; for piercing the flesh, however, the middle;
for piercing the bone, it shall be the highest; but for killing by striking, there is execution.

For cutting off the ears, nose, or hands, for breaking teeth, or for piercing bones, the middle amercement shall be imposed; however, it shall be double in the case of those who have fallen from their caste.

For the cutting off of the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine shall be imposed; for the piercing [or mutilating] of these, the middle fine is prescribed by the teacher.
But for one who has already been sentenced, the punishment prescribed for physical assault is applied;
if [the stolen object] is taken, it is doubled, and the royal fine is even greater than that.
In cases of breaking a limb, causing pain, or likewise cutting it off,
the offender shall be made to pay the expenses for recovery, as well as whatever was seized during the quarrel.
If one who has been struck or seen to be killed is found in a secluded place,
the killer should be identified either by inference or by means of an oath.
Whether inside a house or in a forest, at night or wherever blood is seen where one has been struck, one should not question witnesses in that case.
Someone, having made a mark upon himself, might attack another out of malice;
since this may be done for a specific motive through excessive capabilities, it is proper to investigate the matter therein.
A man who, when reviled, reviles in return; when struck, strikes back;
or who kills one who has committed an offense against him, does not thereby become free from guilt.
Likewise, those born in the reverse order (prātilomya) and the lowest castes are remembered as the impurities among men;
they are to be executed for an offense against a Brahmin, but never should wealth be given to them.
He who causes oxen to be driven at an improper time when they are exhausted, afflicted by hunger, or thirsty,
must perform the same expiation as a cow-killer, or else be made to pay a fine.
He who initiates a quarrel shall be made to pay the costs of its commencement and whatever was expended for it; furthermore,
if a Śūdra strikes members of the twice-born in anger with any limb,
that very limb of his must be cut off— so it has been declared by Manu.
Thieves are recorded as being of two kinds: those who act openly and those who act in secret.
Through the various powers of their intellect, they are divided into a thousand types.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.22.1–2] Those who steal by means of light and darkness; professional gamblers, physicians, and cheats; those who bribe members of an assembly and deceivers;
those who know of divine portents and omens; those who appear auspicious; craftsmen and counterfeiters.
Those who do not perform their duties, those who remain indifferent, false witnesses, open thieves, and likewise those who live by deception— these indeed are public robbers.
Those who break through walls, those who rob travelers, those who steal bipeds and quadrupeds,
those who snatch away [goods], and those who steal crops— these should be known as secret thieves.
When they have been identified by the king’s officers through their associations, signs, or appearances,
they shall be made to restore what was stolen and be punished with the penalties prescribed by the scriptures.
But one who steals a weaver's shuttle should be torn apart by the king's men with pincers;
a stealer of grain should be made to pay ten times its value as a fine, and double that amount as a penalty.
When the death of a single person of evil conduct brings security to many, his killing bestows merit.
Likewise, O Dawn, one should hang a traveler from a tree by tying him around the neck.
For one who breaks a sealed knot on a finger, the king should have the offending finger cut off at the first offense;
at the second, both hands and feet; at the third, he deserves the death penalty.
But that physician who, ignorant of medicinal herbs and mantras and lacking true knowledge of disease,
takes wealth from the sick, shall be punished like a thief.
The gambling must be conducted openly; those who cheat at dice shall be banished.
Those who play with false dice, the base, those who seize the wives of kings, fraudulent astrologers, and gamblers— all these are declared to be punishable.
Furthermore, a merchant who sells refined goods that are mixed with concealed defects shall be made to pay double the value of those goods, as well as a fine for the merchant equal to that amount.
Those members of the assembly who speak unjustly, as well as those who live on bribes and those who deceive the trusting— all of them must be banished.
Those who, out of greed for wealth, proclaim to people knowledge of astrology as well as portents without having understood them, should be restrained with effort.
Those who display themselves as being endowed with the staff, the deerskin, and other such emblems,
yet secretly injure men, are to be put to death by the king’s officers.
Those who, by means of processing, turn an article of small value into one of great value,
and those who deceive women and children, shall be punished in proportion to the value of the object.
But those who manufacture artificial gold, pearls, coral, and so forth,
shall be made to pay the purchaser the price and a fine double that amount by the king.
When neutral witnesses deceive one party out of affection, greed,
or other such motives, or when witnesses give false testimony, they shall be made to pay a fine double the amount in dispute.
Those who, through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, display some form of delusion or perform root-rites (mūlakarman) shall be banished by the king.
One who breaks a joint, one who steals, and those who must be abandoned should then be impaled upon a stake;
likewise, a traveler caught at dawn should be bound by the neck and suspended from a tree.
Those who carry off human beings should be burned by the king with a fire of straw;
one who steals a cow should have his nose cut off, or, having been bound, he should be submerged in water.
For stealing more than ten jars of grain, the punishment is death;
for lesser amounts, he shall be made to pay eleven times its value, and that property must be restored to its owner.
One who steals grain shall be made to pay ten times its value as a fine; for stealing gold or silver, he shall be made to pay twice that amount.
Whether it be grass, or wood, or a flower, or a fruit—
one who takes any of these without having asked permission deserves the amputation of a hand.
One who has committed theft while being devoted to his conduct and Vedic study shall suffer long in prison;
he must restore that wealth to its owner, but no penance is to be performed for him.
This is declared for all thieves regarding the infliction of punishment.
Now, let the proper punishment for violence be heard.
Killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
and both forms of harsh speech— these constitute the fourfold category of *sāhasa* (violent crimes).
That [discipline] is proclaimed to be of three kinds—inferior, middling, and superior.
In that regard, the first, the best, and the middling depend upon the nature of the substance and upon self-restraint.
The wise declare that these practices are to be avoided in the Kali age: the killing of foremost brahmins who are aggressors in a righteous war.
One who destroys or steals the implements of a field, a boundary marker, or the roots, flowers, and fruits [of that field] shall be fined one hundred panas according to the nature of the offense.
One who destroys livestock, clothing, food, drink, or household utensils should be made to pay for them like a thief, as well as a fine of two hundred panas.
For women, men, gold, gems, as well as the property of gods or Brahmins,
and for silken cloth or other superior articles, the fine shall be equal to their value.
Or rather, kings should determine a double fine in consideration of the person;
or else, the killer should be executed to prevent a recurrence of such incidents.
Violence is said to be of five kinds, among which killing is considered the gravest. Those who commit such acts should not be punished with fines; they must be executed with diligence.
Those who are open assassins as well as those who are assassins by stealth—
having identified them and having seized their wealth, they should be executed by various means of death.
Whether for the sake of gaining a friend or acquiring wealth, a king who desires the welfare of the world must not release perpetrators of violence,
for they bring fear to all people.
If a king, out of greed or fear, does not punish those who act unjustly,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is deprived of his sovereignty.
That man who causes the death of others by means of confinement, fire, poison, or weapons,
motivated by anger or other such causes, is a perpetrator of violence (sāhasika).
[The Determination of Joint Assault] Where many people, filled with rage, strike at one person, he who delivers the blow to a vital spot is declared the killer. Br̥h. 1.23.14.
But he who strikes their vital points shall be made to pay the fine as previously stated;
likewise the instigator, the accomplice, the one who points out the way,
the shelterer, the giver of weapons, and the giver of food to those who commit forbidden acts.
One who instructs in war, one who demonstrates its destruction, one who is indifferent, one who is engaged in the task, one who speaks of faults, and one who approves [of them]. // Brh_1.23.16 //
One who kills an assassin shall never incur sin for that killing; one who causes the death of an approaching person seeking his destruction commits no offense. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.23.3, 17)

He who does not kill an assassin— even one who is superior and endowed with good conduct and Vedic study— when that assassin has reached the point of being slain, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
If one kills an assailant who is born of noble family and devoted to Vedic study, by not killing him he would be a killer of an embryo; by killing him, he does not become a killer of an embryo.
Now, hear about the rash act of theft born of anger and greed,
as well as the determination [of guilt] when the perpetrator is not seen:
a slight wound, the absence of a blow, and careful examination of the vital spots.
Having ascertained both his capability and his disposition through various signs, one should win him over with favor.
But where a person is seen slain while the slayer is not seen,
he should be identified by the king according to his previous enmity.
But he who is the actual slayer among them shall be made to pay the penalty as stated;
the one who provides the means and the accomplice shall each receive half of that penalty.
His neighbors— both those living next door and those further away— as well as his friends, enemies, and kinsmen,
should be questioned by the king’s officers using conciliation and other such means.
He may be identified by men through association with the wicked or by means of stolen property;
this has been declared as the method for discerning murderers and thieves.
But he who, having been apprehended on suspicion, does not proceed to fulfill that task, must be cleared by an oath; this is the rule in all such cases.
One who is purified by divine means becomes pure; one who is impure deserves execution.
Through punishment and favor, the king’s fame and righteousness increase.
Harshness is said to be of two kinds, and violence is characterized by two types; learn now that adultery, which is the root of evil, is of three varieties. *Bṛhadaranyaka Upaniṣad* 1.24.1.
Two types [of love] are produced by external conditions, while the third arises from passion;
that, moreover, is said to be threefold: inferior, middling, and superior.
That which is done against her will by one who is asleep, intoxicated, or distracted,
or while she is speaking incoherently in private— that indeed is considered "acted under compulsion."
When a union is brought about by bringing a woman to one's house under false pretenses or by administering intoxicants or magical charms, they know that to be a marriage contracted through fraud.
That which is produced by mutual passion for one's eyes, by the dispatching of female messengers,
and by greed for beauty and wealth, should be known as arising from attachment.
Furthermore, that [approach] is said to be threefold: the initial, the intermediate, and the superior.
Gazing with a sidelong glance, smiling, and likewise sending a female messenger;
touching and gathering her ornaments and garments—this is remembered as the initial [approach].
The sending of perfumes and garlands, incense on the road, clothing,
and private conversation— these they know as the middling means of attraction.
Sharing a bed and a seat, as well as playing, kissing, and embracing—
this is declared by those who know the scriptures to be the highest form of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
The sending of perfumes, garlands, incense, ornaments, and garments,
as well as the enticing with food and drink, is recorded as the middling means of winning over others.
The sending of perfumes, garlands, fruits, food, drink, and clothing,
as well as private conversation, they know to be the middling form of seduction.
And for these three [classes], the first, middle,
and highest forms of discipline should be prescribed, with greater severity applied to those who possess greater wealth.
But a man who engages in conversation with another's wife in private,
having previously been accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement.
One who desires the wealth of a *sahamāya* shall seize all of it;
having cut off his penis and testicles, he shall cause him to be paraded on a donkey.
But he who should desire [another man's wife] through deception shall suffer a fine that seizes all his property;
having been branded with the mark of a female organ, he shall then be banished from the city.

A man who approaches a woman of lower caste when he himself is of higher caste should be led away into the assembly; however, if he approaches a woman of higher caste, his execution must be carried out.
A woman who, having come to a man's house, entices him with touching and other such acts and seeks sexual union there, shall be punished; for the man, half of that fine is prescribed.
One whose nose, lips, and ears have been severed should be made to wander and drown in water,
or be devoured by dogs in a place where many people are assembled.
But if she was enjoyed against her will, he should keep her in his house under guard,
with soiled limbs, sleeping on the ground, and subsisting on a mere morsel of food.
If she has had intercourse with a man of equal caste, he should cause her to perform an expiation such as the Kṛcchra or Parāka penance;
however, if she has been enjoyed by a man of inferior caste, she should either be abandoned or put to death.
This rule for sexual union and the manner of such union has been declared; now hear from me, as I speak, the means by which a woman and a man conduct themselves together. Br̥h. 1.25.1.
A woman must be kept away from even the slightest opportunities for transgression by her own kinsmen;
she must be protected day and night by her mother-in-law and other elder women.
But she who, while indulging her own desires, was not restrained out of affection,
will inevitably come to grief later on, just like a disease that has been neglected.

A father who does not bestow his daughter in marriage at the proper time, a husband who does not approach his wife during her season, and a son who does not provide for his mother when she is in need— all these are blameworthy according to the law and deserve punishment.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
there prosperity, offspring, and purity prevail, and all actions become fruitful.

They should be employed in matters of income and expenditure, the preparation of food, the maintenance of household utensils, cleanliness, and the performance of fire-rituals; this is declared to be the purification for women.
A husband should honor his wife with clothing, ornaments, and food,
especially during festivals, as well as her father, brothers, fathers-in-law, and other kinsmen.
She who does not transgress against her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous.
A woman should not live apart from her husband, father, or sons in another's house;
especially through association with the wicked, she certainly incurs reproach. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.25.2, 9)
Rising before [the elders], serving food and condiments,
and occupying a lower seat or bed— this is declared to be the duty of women toward their gurus.
Excessive drinking, wandering about, sleeping during the day, inactivity, and defiling a woman.
She who is distressed when her husband is distressed, joyful when he is joyful, dejected and emaciated when he is away on a journey,
and who would die when her husband dies— she is to be known as a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
When the master is away on a journey, one should not engage in personal adornment, nor witness dancing, singing, social gatherings, or festivals; nor should one indulge in meat or liquor.
A wife is considered half of one's own body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit;
as long as she lives following her husband, that virtuous woman acts for his welfare.
One who is devoted to vows and fasting, established in celibacy,
and constantly intent on the gift of Dharma, shall go to heaven even if she is childless.

[The Prohibition of Niyoga] Having prescribed *niyoga*, Manu himself prohibited it; because of the decline of the age (*yuga-hrāsa*), this cannot be performed by anyone according to the rules. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.25.3; 1.25.16)
In the Kṛta and Tretā ages, men were endowed with austerity and knowledge;
however, in the Dvāpara and Kali ages, a decline in the power of men has been ordained.
That property which a father gives to his sons, or which is given by him to them, is called *dāya*. Brh_1,26.1 //
One woman should be made to perform work in each house according to her share; many women may be assigned equally. This same rule applies even to female slaves.
Just as water from a well or a pond is drawn out and received according to the size of the vessel,
so too is a field divided by a boundary according to the proportion of the shares.
That must be analyzed through reasoning; otherwise, it would be meaningless.
For those living together under a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods,
and the twice-born shall be one; for those who have divided, that same worship shall be performed in each individual household.
Witnessing, acting as a guarantor, giving, and receiving—these brothers who have divided their inheritance may perform among themselves; those who have not divided it may not.
Those among whom these transactions regarding their own inheritance take place in the world should be understood as divided, even in the absence of a written document.
The obstruction of the family lineage is known as *bodha*; it establishes one in rashness.
It is the separate wealth resulting from the division of one's own immovable property for personal enjoyment.

The division of property among brothers in the absence of the parents has been fully explained; it occurs when the mother’s menses have ceased and the sisters have been given away in marriage. *Bṛhad-āraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.26.2, 9.
[The Order of Partition] Regarding houses and fields acquired by inheritance, the sons have equal shares.
Sons are not entitled to a partition of paternal property against the father's will.
Those sons of the twice-born who are born of wives of equal caste shall divide the estate equally after giving a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the eldest.
Through age, learning, and austerity, one indeed receives two shares of the wealth;
for as the wealth obtained through partition is put to the purpose of sacrifice,
so should the learned increase the weight of those shares.
Their sons, whether equal or unequal [in number], are traditionally held to be the heirs to their father's share.
Regarding property acquired by the grandfather, whether it be immovable or movable,
equal ownership has indeed been declared for both the father and the son.
If shares have been assigned by the father that are either equal, deficient, or excessive, they must be maintained exactly as they were; otherwise, those sons would be subject to correction.
But in the division [of property] while [the father] is still living, the father shall take two shares for himself.
The division of inheritance among heirs is proclaimed to be of two kinds:
one according to the order of seniority by age, and the other an equal distribution of shares.
But whatever is acquired by those who are united, all of them are entitled to equal shares therein;
their sons, whether of unequal or equal status, are declared to be the inheritors of their father's share.
All sons who inherit their father’s estate are entitled to equal shares;
however, among them, one who is devoted to learning and virtuous action deserves to receive more.
He by whom fame is established and celebrated here in this world for the sake of learning, discernment, and valor, and in the acts of bestowing knowledge— by him his ancestors have truly found a son.
The eldest by virtue of birth, learning, and qualities shall receive two shares from the inheritance;
the others, however, shall share equal portions, but he who is equal to his father [in merit] shall take that [entire share].
In her absence, however, the mother shares an equal portion with the sons;
the mothers receive equal shares, and the daughter receives a fourth share. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.22)
For unmarried daughters, however, a fourth share is prescribed;
for sons, there are three shares. But equality is ordained when the wealth is small.
If many sons are born of one [mother] and are equal in their number within that birth-group,
they must divide their own property according to the share of the mother, in accordance with the law.
Among those who are of the same caste but differ in number, the share of the males is prescribed;
however, all paternal grandmothers are declared to be equal to mothers.

But those among them who have not yet undergone the sacramental rites are to be consecrated by their elder brothers from the paternal wealth alone, as are the unmarried daughters, according to the prescribed rule.
But those brothers who are uninitiated and younger than others should indeed be initiated by their elder brothers from the paternal wealth remaining after the middle portion has been set aside.
And he should give sufficient wealth, or a portion of land, according to his wish.
Whether by a married woman or by an unmarried girl, that which is obtained from her husband, from her father’s house,
from her brother, or from her parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (a woman's separate property).
Having obtained her dowry, independence is prescribed for women,
because that was given by their [relatives] as a means of subsistence out of compassion.

In both sale and gift, even regarding immovable property, the woman's wealth shall belong to her offspring; and the daughter shall be entitled to a share thereof. If she is unmarried, she receives it; but if she is married, she receives only honor.
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal uncle’s wife,
a father’s sister, a mother-in-law, and the wife of an elder brother are proclaimed to be equal to one’s own mother.
If these women have neither a son born of their own body nor a daughter’s son,
then their wealth shall be inherited by their sister’s sons, from whom those [women] received it.
Even a son born of a wife of the same caste, if he lacks good qualities, is not entitled to his father's wealth; rather,
that property is ordained for those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) who offer him the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
A son protects his father from creditors, both those who are superior and those who are inferior;
however, if it is otherwise than this, there is no purpose served by him.
What is done with that cow which neither yields milk nor is pregnant? What is the purpose of a son being born who is neither learned nor righteous? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.36)
A son who lacks valor in learning, is devoid of wealth, is bereft of austerity and wisdom,
and is destitute of proper conduct, is considered equal to urine and excrement.

Even with regard to immovable property and bipeds, even if acquired by oneself, there can be neither gift nor sale without having assembled all the sons. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.5) [The Division of Sons] (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.38)
Those humans who have been born, those yet to be born, those dwelling in the womb, and those residing with their ancestors—all of them desire that livelihood; therefore, it must not be cut off.

Household utensils, vehicles, and the like, as well as food, ornaments, and servants, are divided when they are visible; however, when they are hidden, a hair-parting (keśa) is prescribed [as the means of division].
Those born of the Kṣatriya order receive three, two, or one shares; those born of the Vaiśya order, however, receive two and one shares respectively.
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are born from the Brahmin in due order;
they shall possess four, three, two, and one shares respectively.
One born of a Śūdra woman by a twice-born man does not deserve a share of land;
rather, the twice-born man shall receive everything—thus is the law established.
Those sons of theirs who are of the same caste (savarna) shall share a third part of the inheritance;
those who are of a lower caste shall live with him, provided with food and clothing.
For all these sons of one who has no legitimate son (aurasa) are declared to be heirs;
however, once a legitimate son is born, seniority does not remain among them.
That which has been given by the grandfather and the father, as well as that which may have been given by the mother,
and likewise the property acquired through valor or obtained from a wife, must not be taken away from him.
Those who declared that garments and such items are indivisible have not reflected that the wealth of the prosperous consists primarily of clothing and ornaments. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.47)
Having paid off a debt that was recorded in writing... // Bṛh_1.26.48 //
This aforementioned method is indeed to be understood in the case of a debt recorded on a document;
it must be divided by verbal agreement, for otherwise it would be meaningless.
That which stands in the middle and cannot sustain life cannot be given to a single person;
it must be divided with reason, otherwise it would become useless.
Having sold clothing and ornaments, having collected wealth by means of a written contract,
and having exchanged prepared food for unprepared food, [the property] is then divided.
The acquisition of property belonging to those who share in security and well-being should be divided equally;
and the heirs must always manage its use according to their respective shares.
If a son of a Brahmin woman takes land that has become a religious endowment (brahmadāya), or a house, or ancestral field, all the twice-born [kinsmen] shall take it away. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.26.53)
Those who have been partitioned from their father— whether they be stepbrothers or uterine brothers,
or even those who are junior— they are the ones who shall take the father’s share.
The first-born son has no independent power over his paternal inheritance; one born after partition has no claim on the share of his brothers.

Whatever was acquired by the father himself after he had divided his property with his sons, all that belongs to the son born after the partition; it is traditionally held that the earlier-born sons have no claim to it.
Just as with wealth, so it is with debt, and in matters of giving, receiving, and buying;
they have no mutual authority over one another, except regarding impurity and the water-libation rites.
Regarding that which was seized from the grandfather, that which was acquired by the father through his own power,
and that which was obtained through learning, valor, and so forth— the ownership therein is declared to belong to the father.
One may freely give away gifts and likewise enjoy wealth from that property;
in its absence, sons are declared to be entitled to equal shares.
Having honored with perfumes and garlands the father’s garments, ornaments, bed, vehicle, and so forth, one should present them to the recipient of the śrāddha meal.
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do divide them fall.
By the grace of their father, they enjoy garments and ornaments.
Whether the partition has been made or not, if an heir who is entitled to inherit asserts that the property is common, he shall indeed be the one to receive the share.
He whose debt, document, house, or field belongs to his grandfather shall receive his share even if he has been away for a long time, provided he returns.
If one who has abandoned the common ancestral property (gotrasādhāraṇa) takes refuge in another region,
a share must undoubtedly be given to him when he returns, even if only halfway.
Whether it be the third, the fifth, or even the seventh [generation],
if the births [of the ancestors] are not fully known, one shall receive the share according to the order of succession.
When all the primary kinsmen know through tradition that the deceased was the owner,
then the land must be given to his successor who has arrived, by those of the same lineage.
When undivided kinsmen who were previously divided live together again, a further partition of the inheritance shall take place up to the fourth generation; this is the settled rule.
The sons have been divided in many ways by the ancient seers;
they cannot be divided now by those who are long-lived and devoid of such power.
The legitimate son of the body alone is declared the sole owner of the paternal wealth;
the son of an appointed daughter is equal to him, while all others are remembered as those who must be maintained.
But other sons, such as the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) and the rest, are entitled to five, six, or seven shares.
The son given, the abandoned, the purchased, the made, and likewise the Śūdra-born—
these are all considered middle sons, pure by birth, and heirs to the estate.

The son born of the wife (kṣetraja), as well as the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the maiden-born son (kānīna), the son received with the bride (sahoḍha), the son secretly born (gūḍhaja), and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāsuta) are condemned by the virtuous.
The son of a Śūdra woman who has been self-given, and those who are recorded as being purchased—all these are declared to be mere friends; they are undoubtedly *kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas*.
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes to the family of another, becomes by that misconduct a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*; of this there is no doubt.
Gautama said that [the practice] is performed after sacrificing to Agni and Prajāpati;
however, others say that for one who has no son, a daughter may be designated as a son (putrikā) by intention.
Thirteen types of sons were previously declared by Manu;
among them, the legitimate son (aurasa) and the appointed daughter (putrikā) are the causes for the continuation of the lineage.
Just as oil is remembered by the wise as a substitute for clarified butter when the latter is unavailable,
so too are the eleven types of sons considered substitutes for the appointed daughter (putrikā) and the legitimate son of the body (aurasa).
If there are many uterine brothers born of one father,
then when a son is born to even one of them, they are all considered to have sons.
This same rule is prescribed for many wives who have one husband;
if among them only one has sons, he alone is the giver of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) for all of them.
Since a son protects his father from the hell named Put,
he should strive for his birth even by means of merely looking upon his face.
Now, both the grandson and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) bring about the attainment of heaven;
they are declared to be equal in regard to the inheritance of property and the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
And if the father has died, those born of a Śūdra wife who were taken as concubines out of lust shall give to their brother only a share for the sake of honor, provided that he is obedient.
For the sake of food, one *prastha* of rice with fuel should be given in the afternoon;
and a garment purchased for three *paṇas* should be given once every three months.
[Br̥h 1,26.8 vidhavābhāgaḥ] Only this much is prescribed as the property of a widow for virtuous women. Br̥h 1,26.85.
Having set aside the wealth for clothing, food, and likewise for the washerman,
one should allot what remains to the heirs.
Now, for one who has no son, a wife of noble birth or even daughters are prescribed;
in their absence, the father, mother, brother, and sons are declared [to be the heirs].
A man without a son should, with diligent effort, adopt a son of whatever kind may be available,
for the sake of performing the rites of offering rice-balls and water, and for the proclamation of his religious merit.
The ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for sons, thinking:
"Whoever goes to Gayā will deliver us."
Just as a man who attempts to cross water with a leaky boat sinks,
so too does a father sink into blinding darkness because of a wicked son.
He will perform the rite of releasing a bull, as well as sacrifices and works of public utility;
in his old age, he will protect [the earth] and offer ancestral oblations every day.
In the Vedic tradition, in the systems of law (Smṛti), and in worldly custom,
the wise have declared that a wife is half of one's body, sharing equally in the fruits of both merit and demerit.
For one whose wife has not passed away, half of his body lives;
while half of the body is living, how could another take possession of the wealth?
But when there are kinsmen— paternal uncles, brothers, or blood relations—
the wife of one who has died without a son shall take that inheritance.
If the husband has died while the *agnihotra* was previously maintained, the devoted wife shall inherit that wealth; this is the eternal law.
A barren woman shall take the fire; one who has ascended [the funeral pyre] shall remove the sin.
In the absence of sons, the wife shall be the heir; in the absence of the wife, the uterine brother;
in his absence, the kinsman (dāyāda); and after that, the daughter's son shall inherit the wealth.
Having taken moving and stationary property, gold, silver, grain, liquids, and clothing,
one should cause the śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other rites to be performed.

One should honor paternal uncles, teachers, daughters' sons, sisters' husbands, maternal uncles, elders, guests, and women with offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and with works of public utility (pūrta).
Whatever was previously ordained by rule regarding the ancestral property (ādhi) and so forth when the wealth had been divided,
that the wife shall receive upon her husband’s death, with the exception of immovable property.
Even if she has been established in her duties and even if a portion [of the estate] has been assigned, a woman does not deserve immovable property.
If a widow becomes harsh while still in the prime of youth,
then a livelihood must be provided for the purpose of sustaining her life.
Upon the death of her husband, a woman who protects her family shall receive her husband’s share;
for as long as she lives, she possesses no ownership over it regarding its gift, mortgage, or sale.
A woman who has been purchased for the sake of sexual enjoyment by one desiring offspring,
or who has been taken from another, is indeed declared to be a wife.
Or indeed, one should give a funeral ball (piṇḍa) or a portion of land according to one's own will.
That means of subsistence from immovable property which has been given by the father-in-law to women cannot be taken away by others once the father-in-law has died.
Those sapindas or kinsmen who act as obstacles to her and would seize her wealth, the king shall cause them to be executed with the punishment prescribed for thieves.
[The Division of Reunited Property] Furthermore, those who have reunited out of affection share in each other's portions;
likewise, brothers who were previously divided but live together again in one place out of mutual affection.
Furthermore, when a division is made, no seniority exists among them.
If he should die at some time, or if he should somehow renounce the world, his share is not lost; it is ordained for his uterine brother.
But his sister deserves to receive a share from that [inheritance];
this is the law for one who is childless and lacks both a wife and a father.
Whether she has been given away or not, if a uterine brother dies, she alone shall take his share;
for this is clearly the reason for both cases.
The wealth of each person shall belong to the one who is their nearest sapinda.
If a man has died without offspring, without a wife, and without brothers, father, or mother,
all his *sapiṇḍa* relatives shall divide that inheritance according to their respective shares.
But among those who are co-residents, whoever acquires wealth through learning, valor, or other such means,
two shares of that shall be given to him, and the remainder shall have equal shares.

Furthermore, one who has been divided by his father or brother, yet resides together with him—or with his paternal uncle—out of affection, is called "reunited" (saṃsṛṣṭa). Bṛhad-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.113.
The uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally;
as shall those brothers who are reunited, along with the uterine sisters.
If among them the eldest or the youngest should be deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either one should die, his share is not lost.
But a uterine brother [should give] to a uterine brother;
he should both give a share and take a share for one who is born and for one who has died.
But a uterine brother who is a joint-inheritor shall not take the wealth from one who is not uterine;
even if he is not a joint-inheritor, a uterine brother shall take it, and not one born of a different mother.
But for those whose father has died, the allotment of shares is calculated from the father's side.
Those Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are childless and deprived of wives and brothers—
the king shall take their wealth, for he is indeed the lord of all.

[The distinction among sons according to their caste: A son born to a Brahmin from a Kṣatriya wife, though senior by birth, shall, if endowed with good qualities, receive an equal share with the Kṣatriya; and likewise for one born to a Vaiśya wife.
Land received as a gift must not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or others;
even if their father should give it, when he is dead, the son of a Brahmin shall take it back.
One born from a Śūdra woman by men of the twice-born classes does not deserve a share of land;
he shall receive everything that belongs to his own caste—thus the law is established.
But that Niṣāda who is the only son of a Brahmin shall receive the third share;
then two agnates (sakulyas) or sapindas, being the givers of the funeral oblation (svadhā), shall take [the remainder].
In the absence of a kinsman, the teacher or even the disciple who offers the *svadhā* should likewise provide for those castes in all calamities.
A virtuous son born of a Śūdra womb who serves a childless man shall receive a maintenance;
the remaining estate, the sapinda relatives shall obtain.
The wife is the heir to her husband's wealth; in her absence, the daughter is declared to be so.
A daughter is born from every limb of men, just like a son;
therefore, how could any other person take the father's wealth?

But in his absence, if there should be a daughter who is unmarried, then, in the absence of a lineage of sons and grandsons, the daughters' sons shall obtain the wealth. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.128)
Just as one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
Since they both abide within that very self, how could anyone else take away the wealth?
"In this world, according to the law, there is no distinction between a son's son and a daughter's son;
by this very ordinance, he then made his daughter a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter)."
A male is born when the semen is in excess; a female comes into being when the female element is in excess.
A virtuous wife, wedded to a man of equal status, who is devoted to service—
whether she has borne sons or not— is the heir to her father's wealth.
Just as she has ownership over her father’s wealth even while her kinsmen exist,
so too does her son have a right to the wealth of his mother and maternal grandfather.
In their absence, however, the brothers, the sons of the brothers, the uterine kinsmen (sanābhayaḥ),
the distant relatives (sakulyāḥ), the agnates (bāndhavāḥ), the disciples, and those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyāḥ) are entitled to the wealth.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.13: Division of Wealth for One Without Sons] The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies childless;
likewise, she shall obtain it for a son who dies destitute of both wife and children.
The mother should be known as the heir to the inheritance, or the brother with her permission.
In the absence of a son, the wife shall be the heir; in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother;
in his absence, the descendant; and after that, the daughter's son shall inherit the wealth.
From the wealth that has been acquired, one should diligently set aside half of it for the monthly,
six-monthly, or annual *śrāddha* ceremonies.
Where there are many kinsmen, as well as members of the same lineage and relatives,
he who is the nearest among them shall take the wealth of one who has no offspring.
A brother, or a brother’s son, or a sapinda relative, or even a disciple,
having performed the offering of the funeral cakes together, should thereafter perform the rite for prosperity.
Furthermore, he who makes a division according to his own will and then subsequently contradicts it,
shall be made to pay the king’s share from his own property and be punished for the offense.
In the case of denying a joint debt or a deposit,
one should not force the debtor to pay by using fraudulent means or by inflicting injury to his dependents.
Those men who are deceitful, wealthy, cruel,
and greedy should be won over through friendly means, or else by the sacrifice of one's own interests and through guile.
Forceful seizure, ownership of immovable property, prior partition among heirs, and [disputes] where there are no witnesses are to be determined by means of inference. (Br̥haspati 1.26.143)
These transactions of theirs proceed in the world among their own heirs;
one may recognize those who have been divided even without a written document.
And the Vaiśvadeva and other rites must be performed by those who have not separated their property.

The obstruction of the continuity of power, a stolen deposit, acts of violence, the enjoyment of one's own immovable property, and wealth held separately from a partition; these constitute grounds for suspicion.
Those who maintain separate income, expenditure, and assets, and engage with one another in lending,
trade, and commerce, are undoubtedly divided.
The formal document for the proclamation of the partition should be prepared by the brothers who have divided among themselves;
or, when they are dividing, blameless witnesses should be appointed to prevent future disputes.
Whatever portion has been enjoyed by whom, that one shall not displace him from it.

Gambling, which destroys truth, purity, and wealth, was forbidden by Manu; however, when it is conducted by others under the supervision of the king and accompanied by a royal share, it is permitted. Bṛh. 1.27.1.
An activity supervised by a master of the assembly for the purpose of detecting thieves—
this very same rule is to be understood as applying to gambling with living creatures and to betting matches.
[The Conduct of the Master of the Gaming Hall] The master of the gaming hall is the collector there; he shall pay the winnings to the victor and to the king.
The king’s share from the gambling proceeds is ten percent from the master of the gaming hall.
Or it may occur at the appropriate time. ... ... // Brh_1,27.4 //

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.27.2: The Victory and Defeat of the Master] If anyone should suffer defeat in a duel, the master must pay the wager that was stipulated therein. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.27.5)

One who has been defeated in private, or who is ignorant of the matter, or who was deceived by false dice or fraud, must be released; even one who is knowledgeable [of the trickery] shall not be made to pay his entire property, nor shall he be made to pay everything won.

[The Punishment for Fraudulent Gambling] Those wicked gamblers who play with false dice, those who steal the king's share, and those who deceive in counting—these gamblers are declared by tradition to be subject to punishment. Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.27.3; 1.27.7.
Public exposure must be made and fraudulent gamblers shall be banished;
however, one who commits murder shall suffer various forms of capital punishment.
He himself is the witness when the decision regarding victory or defeat is doubtful, provided he is accompanied by three other assessors (*sabhyas*).
When the matter is doubtful for both parties, however, the gamblers themselves are the judges.
But when they become hostile, then the king should investigate.
In this manner, the king should daily oversee the legal disputes brought by litigants,
as well as other matters concerning his subjects, together with learned Brahmins.
When birds, rams, bulls, and other animals, having agreed upon a wager, seize one another and fight, they call that *samāhvaya* (gambling with living creatures). 1.1.28.1.
If anyone should suffer defeat in a duel,
the wager that had been stipulated therein must be paid by his master.

[Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.29, Miscellaneous] This judicial procedure initiated by litigants has been declared in brief; now I shall explain the miscellaneous judicial procedure pertaining to the king.
Having ascertained the nature of the person's fault and their capacity, one should duly impose the fourfold punishment consisting of verbal reprimand, fine, and corporal punishment.
One who deserves death shall be fined one hundred gold pieces;
for one deserving mutilation of a limb, half of that; and for one deserving exile, twenty-five.
The hands, feet, genitals, eyes, tongue, ears, nose, the tip of the tongue, the half-foot, the claspers, the forehead, the lips, the anus, and the hips; Brh_1,29.4 //
These fourteen locations for punishment have been specified;
for a Brahmin, a mark on the forehead is ordained, and no other punishment is prescribed.
One should diligently restrain those who act contrary to dharma by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of intimidation.
But when one is unable to restrain these even by piercing,
then one should employ all four of these methods against them.
One should first apply the punishment of verbal censure, followed by the punishment of "fie" (reproach).
The third is the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal punishment.
And he should place all prisoners along the royal highway,
so that those who have committed evil deeds may be seen there in their suffering and disfigurement.
One who burns the corpse of a person with whom he has no kinship shall take a tenth part of the wealth, or a fifth, or even the whole of it.
Śaunaka says that for one with many wives, it is the tenth [day]; for one with few wives, the fifth; and for one whose father's wife has no son, it is every day.
Likewise, when [a traveler] has departed, one-sixth share and the ferry-toll must be paid;
so too for one who causes dissension in battle, a thief, a traitor, or one who destroys crops.
